firstEdition.headline: A NEW CONCERN
decks: A PROPRIETOR OF REMEDIES OPENS HIS DOORS TO THE AFFLICTED OF THE WARD.
firstEdition.body: A new apothecary has opened on Mulberry street, with one copper still, a shelf of drugs and a dozen regular callers. Its proprietor, who styles himself Dr. ——, informs our reporter that he intends to cure the neighborhood of everything, and that the details are a trade secret. The ward wishes him every success, and has its coughs ready.

rivals.head: DR. GRIMSBY'S GALVANIC BELT
bodies: Worn next the skin. A Current of Health through every Nerve! Sent on thirty days' trial.

bodies.text: Now with Twice the Current! Worn next the skin by Gentlemen of Every Profession. Sent on thirty days' trial.

fines: Wearers are requested not to stand in puddles.
The thirty days' trial is not refundable after the thirty days, or during them.
Not to be worn in a thunderstorm, in the bath, or near a magnet.
Dr. Grimsby regrets that he cannot answer letters asking what the belt is connected to.
Sizes up to fifty inches. Vigor in all sizes.

fines.text: Not to be worn on the trolley, the Company having complained.
A gentleman of Hoboken who wore two at once is said to have lit the hall.
The current is guaranteed; the direction is not.
Now with a second battery, for the gentleman who found the first insufficient.

fines: Returned belts are sold again as new, the proprietor finding no difference.

rivals.head: MRS. PRUDENCE WHITTLE'S VEGETABLE COMPOUND
rivals.body: Write to Mrs. Whittle in strictest confidence. She answers every letter personally.

fines.text: Mrs. Whittle's correspondence continues brisk, notwithstanding her funeral in 'eighty-three.

fines: Mrs. Whittle answers every letter personally, and has done so since her death without complaint.
Mrs. Whittle's portrait is on every bottle. She has not aged a day, and has some reason not to.
Her clerks, of whom there are forty, sign 'P. Whittle' in a fine round hand.

fines.text: Mrs. Whittle's correspondence continues brisk, notwithstanding her funeral ten years ago.
Mrs. Whittle has now answered a million letters, all but the first few from beyond the grave.
Mrs. Whittle's daughters carry on the correspondence, in her name and in her hand.
Mrs. Whittle's advice is free to every lady who writes, and her compound is a dollar to every lady who reads it.
Mrs. Whittle's letters are now answered by type-writer, which she is said to have learned late in life.
Mrs. Whittle was asked by a ladies' magazine to sit for a new portrait, and has sent the old one.

rivals.head: MADAME DE LA ROSE'S ARSENICAL COMPLEXION WAFERS
rivals.body: A Skin of Alabaster! Perfectly Safe! Ladies of Fashion take three daily.
fines: Her complexion was the envy of all who attended the viewing.
Madame de la Rose is at home to callers on Tuesdays, under a veil.
Ladies are advised to take no more than three, and to make their wills before the fourth.
Endorsed by the leading ladies of the stage, two of whom are still on it.
Not to be left where the cat can get them, the cat having no complexion to lose.

fines.text: Now by the hundred, the dozen having proved too few for a lasting effect.
Madame regrets that the wafers cannot be sent by post to Massachusetts, for reasons the Board of Health of that state will explain.
Madame's portrait is retouched by the best photographers in Paris, and her complexion by the same.
Under the new law the label will say what is in them; Madame says it was always there, in French.

rivals.head: PROF. AUGUSTUS BLOOM'S HAIR RESTORER
rivals.body: Rubbed on nightly, it raises hair on billiard balls. Testimonials from the Bald of Three Continents.
fines: Do not apply to the face.
Professor Bloom's own portrait was taken before his experiments began.
Ladies are cautioned against the eyebrows.
Not to be spilt on the carpet, which in the Professor's office is now six inches deep.
Testimonials from a gentleman of Philadelphia who is said to be unrecognised by his own wife.
The Professor's barber says he has never cut so much hair, all of it the Professor's wigs'.

fines.text: Results in thirty days, or the Professor will send a second bottle and thirty days more.
Now perfumed, at the request of the ladies of the boarding-houses where it is used.

rivals.head: PROFESSOR KLINE'S ELECTRIC LIVER PAD
rivals.body: Laid upon the liver, it draws out bile, gloom and torpor by magnetism alone. No medicine required.
fines: Not to be worn near the watch.
The Professor has never seen a liver, but has been told where it is.
Wearers who cannot find the liver may wear it anywhere; it will find the liver.
Sold also as a chest protector, a back plaster and, in summer, a fan.
Beware of imitations, which also do nothing.
The Professor's own liver is said to be in excellent order, having never worn one.

fines.text: Recommended by the Professor's brother, who is a physician, and by the Professor's sister, who is his bookkeeper.

rivals.head: THE ANTI-FAT CORDIAL
bodies: Reduces the figure by a pound a day without diet or exercise. Twelve ladies of Brooklyn have vanished entirely.
Reduces the figure by a pound a day without diet or exercise. A gentleman of Hoboken is now in demand as a lightning-rod.
fines: The proprietors are not responsible for vanished ladies.
Not to be taken by the thin, for fear of the consequences, or by the stout, for fear of the same.
Patrons are advised to stop when satisfied, and to send a friend to say so.
The proprietors, who are all three very stout, take no part in the business but the profits.

fines.text: A lady of Brooklyn took it for a year and is now able to sit in a trolley car, which she has done, and found it no improvement.

fines: The cordial is taken before meals, and the meals are taken anyway.

fines.text: Sold also as a tonic for the thin, in a different bottle.

rivals.head: DR. ST. JOHN'S CONSUMPTION CURE
rivals.body: Cures consumption in all its stages. Testimonials from every state in the Union, and several beyond it.
fines: Several of the testimonials were received posthumously.
Dr. St. John has cured more consumptives than any physician living, he says, and has never lost a patient he heard from again.
Not to be taken with a physician, the two being known to quarrel.
Large bottles one dollar; for the advanced stages, two bottles at once.
Dr. St. John considers the germ theory a foreign notion; his bottle is made in Jersey.

fines.text: Dr. St. John has been invited to address the Tuberculosis Congress, and has declined, being busy.
The sanitariums of the Adirondacks are said to fear it, and the doctor says he fears nothing.

fines: Dr. St. John answers all letters within the week, while there is time.

rivals.head: THE HYGEIA CYCLE TONIC
rivals.body: Restores the Nerve after a Century Run. Endorsed by Seven Clubs of the League of American Wheelmen, or their Secretaries.
fines: Not to be taken while mounted.
A bottle fits the frame of any safety, and the frame of any wheelman.
The League has not endorsed it, and has written to say so; the Secretaries have.

fines.text: Endorsed by the scorchers of the Boulevard, who arrive before it takes effect.

fines: A bottle in each tire, the proprietors say, and the road is no hill.

fines.text: Endorsed by the winner of the six-day race at the Garden, who has not slept since.

rivals.head: PROFESSOR VOLTA'S ELECTRIC INSOLES
rivals.body: A Galvanic Current from Heel to Crown, for Rheumatism, Cold Feet and Low Spirits. Worn by the Crowned Heads of Europe.
fines: The Crowned Heads have not been asked.
Sold in pairs only; the Professor will not answer for a man who walks on one.
A gentleman of Newark who wore them in the rain walked to Philadelphia without meaning to.

fines.text: Not to be worn across the trolley tracks.

fines: The Professor's own boots, he says, have never been off.
Not for the dancing master, several having been unable to stop.

rivals.head: THE ROENTGEN CORSET
rivals.body: Constructed upon the principle of the New Photography. Corrects the Figure and Reveals the Liver.
fines: The Liver is not included.
Ladies are warned that the corset is not responsible for what it reveals.
Endorsed by the X-Ray Laboratories of Paris, which the proprietor has seen in a photograph.
A lady of Murray Hill who wore it to the photographer's has had the plate destroyed.
The rays pass through the corset; the proprietor's price does not.

rivals.head: RADIOLENE
rivals.body: Liquid Sunshine, charged with the Wonder-Element of Madame Curie. Glows in the Bottle and in the Patient.
fines: Keep from the photographic plates.
Each bottle certified to glow, by a gentleman who glows himself.
Not to be kept by the bed, patients having complained of the light.
Every bottle guaranteed to contain Radium, or a word very like it.

fines.text: Under the new law the label will declare its contents: Water, and Enthusiasm.

fines: A chemist of the College of Pharmacy who examined a bottle found it very like the Croton, but warmer.

fines.text: Now in the half-dark bottle, so the glow can be seen in daylight.

fines: The proprietor has offered a bottle to Madame Curie, who has not replied.

rivals.head: DR. SPRY'S MOTOR NERVE TONIC
rivals.body: Steadies the Hand at Twenty Miles an Hour. Recommended to all who own, drive, or have been run down by a Motor-Car.
fines: Twenty miles an hour is not recommended.
The Automobile Club does not endorse it, its members preferring to be run down by something else.
Sold at the garages, and at the police station, where the automobilists wait for their hearing.
Not to be confused with the gasoline, though the proprietor has.
Taken by the chauffeurs of Fifth avenue, who are said to need it more than the owners.
A bottle under the seat, and the horses on the road are no longer a worry.

fines.text: The Speed Law is no concern of the tonic's, the proprietor says, the tonic having never been arrested.

rivals.head: THE PASTEUR PURE-MILK TABLETS
rivals.body: Dissolve one in the Baby's Milk and the Microbe Flees. Scientifically Proven upon a Large Number of Babies.
fines: The number is not stated.
The Board of Health has tested the tablets and found them to be chalk. The proprietors say it is a very pure chalk.
The milk should be boiled as well, the proprietors concede, the tablets being a supplement to boiling.
Endorsed by a professor of Vienna, whose practice is chiefly in the advertising columns.
M. Pasteur has not been asked, and is not expected to be.

fines.text: Recommended for the milk of the Greater City, Brooklyn's included, which the proprietors call the harder case.
The Department's pure milk depots are said to be ruining the tablet trade, out of jealousy.

rivals.head: TEXAS JACK WILDER'S PRAIRIE BITTERS
rivals.body: Compounded from Herbs Known Only to the Red Man, and to Texas Jack, who Was Told. Sold from the Wagon and by All Druggists.
fines: The Red Man has not been asked, and has not been paid.
Texas Jack learned the secret from a chief whose name he has forgotten and whose tribe he has mislaid.
Texas Jack has never been to Texas, but has seen a picture of it.
Bottled in Jersey City, from the Prairie.
Texas Jack rides in the parade on Decoration Day, on a horse hired from a livery in Hoboken.

fines.text: Texas Jack's Wild West is said to be coming to Madison Square Garden, as soon as he has found one.
Now with the portrait of Texas Jack in his later years, the first having worn off the plate.

rivals.head: DR. HARTWELL'S CATARRH SNUFF
rivals.body: A Pinch in each Nostril and the Catarrh is Forgotten, and so, for an Hour, is Everything Else.
fines: Thousands of satisfied users ask for it by the box, and some by the hour.
Not habit-forming, the proprietor says, and says it again, very quickly.
The Board of Pharmacy has asked what is in it; Dr. Hartwell has asked the Board what is in theirs.
Taken by the pinch, by the spoon and, in the advanced cases, by the dollar's worth.

fines.text: Under the new law the box must say cocaine, which Dr. Hartwell says he always meant it to.
The druggists of the Tenderloin report a heavy demand, chiefly at night.

rivals.head: DR. ASHBY'S CRIMSON PELLETS FOR THE PALLID
rivals.body: Make Pale People Pink, Pink People Rosy, and Rosy People Write to Us. Fifty Cents the Box.
fines: A lady of Yonkers took the full course and now matches her curtains.
The pellets are the color of health; the proprietors have not been able to obtain the thing itself.
Pale people are asked to send their portraits, before and after; the after is colored by hand.
The pellets are now coated, the color having come off on the hands of several customers and on the gloves of one.

fines.text: Recommended by the shop-girls of Sixth avenue, who are given a box at Christmas in lieu of a raise.

rivals.head: PROFESSOR MARVIN'S MAGIC LINIMENT
rivals.body: Cures Rheumatism, Neuralgia, Lame Back and Melancholy. A Concert of Song from the Wagon, Every Evening, Free.
fines: The songs are free; the liniment is extra, and so is leaving before the end.
Applied outwardly for the pain, and inwardly, the Professor says, for the singing.
The Professor's wagon is licensed as a concert, a pharmacy and, in two states, a nuisance.
The Professor's banjo player is said to be the best in the trade, and the only member of the company paid in cash.
Rub well in, and the Professor will rub it in further next week, from the same wagon.

classifieds.text: PERSONAL.—Will the proprietor who left a crate of his Elixir on the steps of the Foundling Asylum on Thursday, for the babies, please call for the crate. The Sisters have the babies in hand.

classifieds: FOR SALE.—Bottles, a gross, embossed CURE. Will scrape off for an extra cent.
WANTED.—Agents in every town to sell a remedy on commission. No knowledge of medicine needed, or wanted.
NOTICE.—The undersigned will not be responsible for debts contracted by his wife while under the influence of any remedy.
WANTED.—A DOCTOR'S CARRIAGE, second hand. The doctor is not required.
WANTED.—A LECTURER for a medicine wagon, of good voice and no fixed opinions. Must ride, sing and be gone by morning. Apply after dark, Chatham square.
WANTED.—A LADY of fine figure to be photographed 'after.' The 'before' is already engaged.
FOR SALE.—A druggist's business, old established, with good will and stock; the proprietor retiring on account of an inquest. Apply at the side door.
WANTED.—An OLD GENTLEMAN of venerable appearance to sit in a window with a long beard and a bottle. No talking.
LOST.—A testimonial, signed, from a gentleman since deceased. Of no use to the finder, the gentleman not being available to sign another.
WANTED.—A CHEMIST who can make a brown liquid taste like medicine. Must not ask what it is for. Fair wages, and a share of the silence.
TO LET.—A good corner, with a doctor's sign, two stone mortars and a brass pestle, all ornamental.
WANTED.—HAIR, human, all shades, for the before-and-after portraits of a hair restorer. The after is wanted urgently.
FOR SALE.—A Galvanic Belt, worn twice. The owner survived the first wearing and does not wish to risk a second.
WANTED.—A BOY to lick labels, and a second boy to watch the first. References.
SITUATION WANTED.—By a former coroner's juryman of long experience, as watchman, porter or anything not requiring an opinion.
WANTED.—A CORRESPONDENT of either sex to answer the letters of the late Dr. ——, who continues to receive them. Must write a medical hand.
LOST.—The formula of a celebrated remedy, written on a shirt cuff. The proprietor offers ten dollars; the laundry has been searched.
WANTED.—A PARROT that can say 'It cured me.' Must say nothing else; the last parrot did.
FOUND.—A wooden leg, in Mulberry street, near the shop of a celebrated rheumatism cure. The owner is evidently cured, and may call for it.
WANTED.—EMPTY BOTTLES with the labels on. The labels are particularly wanted. Apply to a gentleman entering the trade.
WANTED.—A NURSE for an infant that will not sleep. No soothing syrups: the last three nurses used them, and the infant is now the only one in the house awake.
FOR SALE.—A celebrated name for a remedy, never used, with a crest. Apply to a printer of Ann street, who has a dozen.
MATRIMONIAL.—A gentleman of means, in the medicine way, wishes to meet a lady of fine complexion who asks no questions. Object, a testimonial.
WANTED.—A GENTLEMAN in a clerical collar to stand near a medicine wagon and look grave. The collar is supplied.
WANTED.—Old almanacs of any patent medicine, for wrapping. Last year's are as good as this year's, the weather not having changed.
MONEY WANTED.—Fifty dollars, by a proprietor on the point of a great success, at any interest. Security, the success.
WANTED.—A STRONG WOMAN to carry a remedy up five flights of tenement stairs, twice a day, and say nothing on the way down.
FOR SALE.—A quantity of testimonials, slightly used, from the counties of New Jersey. Names may be changed to suit.
WANTED.—A COOK who can make a dinner the doctor would forbid. Apply to a gentleman who has found a remedy for dyspepsia.
TO LET.—A pew, Rivington street, near the door; suitable for a proprietor who leaves early.
WANTED.—A LOUD BOY to cry a remedy in the streets. Must not believe in it; the last boy did, and took it.
FOUND.—In a Bowery car, a bottle of a celebrated tonic, full. Supposed to have been left by a gentleman who had read the label.
WANTED.—A BOOKKEEPER who can keep two sets of books and remember which is which. Apply to a silent partner.
WANTED.—A SMART YOUNG MAN to fold almanacs. Need not read them; nobody does.

classifieds.text: WANTED.—A TYPE-WRITER, young lady, to copy testimonials. The machine is supplied; the testimonials are not.
WANTED.—INDIAN MEDICINE MEN, two, for a summer tour of New Jersey. Must look Indian from a wagon. Feathers found.
WANTED.—A smart lad with a high wheel to deliver bottles. Must be able to get down.
WANTED.—A YOUNG MAN on a bicycle to ride slowly past the shop wearing a sign. Must not scorch.
FOR SALE.—A lady's bicycle, nearly new, with bloomers. The lady has been cured of it.
WANTED.—A strong voice to speak a testimonial into a phonograph. Will be played eleven hundred times; must not cough.
WANTED.—A RECRUIT for Cuba to carry a bottle of a tonic and say so. Return passage guaranteed, if he returns.
WANTED.—Half-tone portraits of persons restored to health. The persons need not be present.
WANTED.—A SANDWICH, any condition, by a hotel of Elizabeth street under the new law. The old one has given out.
WANTED.—A CHAUFFEUR to drive a medicine wagon without a horse. Must be able to lecture at fifteen miles an hour.
WANTED.—A CHEMIST to tell a proprietor what is in his remedy before the Government does. Strictly confidential.
WANTED.—NEW LABELS, any quantity, by the first of January, plain type, saying as little as the law allows. Apply to any proprietor.
WANTED.—A little radium, or anything that glows, for a tonic. Will pay well for either.
WANTED.—A MOVING-PICTURE MAN to make a film of a cure. The cure will take place before the camera, in one minute.
TO LET.—A store over the new subway station; the trade passes under it all day.
SITUATION WANTED.—By a member of the late Poison Squad, as taster for a remedy. Has eaten worse.
LOST.—A telephone number, in Grand street. The finder is asked not to ring it; the druggist is not at home to the Board of Health.
WANTED.—A STENOGRAPHER to take down testimonials at the counter as they are given, and improve them.
FOR SALE.—An automobile, steam, nearly new; also a horse, which the owner kept in case.
WANTED.—Picture post cards of persons cured, any town. Will pay a cent each and the postage.
WANTED.—A YOUNG MAN with a good hand to address circulars to the afflicted. Must not be afflicted himself. Box 41, this office.
WANTED.—A LADY TYPEWRITER to copy testimonials. Must type faster than they can be written. Apply to a proprietor, rear building.

LOST.—A photograph of a gentleman before taking a hair restorer. The photograph of him after is not wanted. Reward.
WANTED.—Testimonials in Italian, Yiddish and German, for a remedy whose proprietor speaks none of them. Liberal terms. Box 72, this office.
TO LET.—A store with a window on the Bowery, lately a druggist's. The fixtures go with it, and the smell.

WANTED.—An ELECTRICIAN to wire a liniment. Box 50, this office.
WANTED.—A boy to stand outside a shop on Fourteenth street and look ill until a lady passes, then well. Apply in the morning, before breakfast.

TO LET.—A cellar, dry, suitable for the manufacture of a remedy. Apply to the landlord, who will not ask which.
WANTED.—A BOOKKEEPER who can keep two sets of books and remember which is which. Box 2, this office.
WANTED.—A COPY OF THE NEW FOOD AND DRUG LAW, in plain English, by a proprietor who has been told it is in plain English. Box 11, this office.
WANTED.—A RESPECTABLE ELDERLY LADY to answer to the name of a remedy's grandmother, for a portrait. Must not have been anyone's grandmother in particular.
WANTED.—Moving pictures of a gentleman restored to health, for a nickel show. The gentleman will be supplied.
LOST.—A bottle of a remedy for the memory. The owner cannot say where.

timeline_end.headline: THE LAW ARRIVES
decks: The Pure Food and Drug Act.
FROM THE FIRST OF JANUARY, EVERY BOTTLE MUST SAY WHAT IS IN IT.
timeline_end.body: The new federal law takes effect this week. Proprietors of remedies must now declare upon the label any alcohol, morphine, opium, cocaine, heroin, eucaine, chloroform, cannabis, chloral hydrate or acetanilide their preparations contain. The proprietor of {product} told our reporter that he welcomed the measure, and has ordered a great many new labels.

standing: POLICE COURT.—Patrick Hagan, 40, was fined two dollars for being drunk on Mott street. He told the Justice he had taken nothing but a tonic, and named it. The Justice fined the tonic also.

standing.text: SHIPPING.—Arrived, the steamer Wyoming, from Liverpool, with 612 steerage and three cases of a patent pill for the trade. Both were landed.

standing: A CARD.—The undersigned begs to inform his friends that he is not the Dr. —— of Mulberry street, and has never been, and will thank the ward to stop asking him for it.

standing.text: SPORTING.—At Harry Hill's on Saturday, a sparring exhibition, four rounds, for a purse of ten dollars. The loser was revived with a remedy and is said to be doing well.

standing: LOST.—On the Bowery, a gentleman's umbrella with a horn handle. Also his health, which he believes he left at a druggist's. Reward for the umbrella.

standing.text: THE WEATHER.—The Signal Service predicts fair and colder. Druggists report the colder part already selling well.

standing: BOARDING.—A quiet front room for a single gentleman of regular habits. No cooking, no dogs, no remedies in the room.
THE ELEVATED.—The Third Avenue line reports eleven passengers asleep at the terminus on Sunday, a record. All were roused but two, who were thought to be resting.

standing.text: SPORTING.—The pedestrian match at the Garden enters its fifth day. The leader attributes his endurance to cold water and a clear conscience, and is not expected to win.

standing: A CARD.—Mrs. E. Dooley wishes to thank the neighbors for their kindness during her late husband's illness, and the druggist on the corner for his.
WANTED.—A strong boy to carry bottles. Must not drink from them. Apply at the back.
AMUSEMENTS.—At a theatre on the Bowery, "The Poisoned Chalice," a drama in five acts. The management guarantees every death in it is a stage death.
FOUND.—In Chatham square, a purse containing forty cents and a recipe. The finder has kept the forty cents.

POLICE COURT.—A woman was charged with taking a bottle of soothing syrup from a counter in Hester street. The court, on learning the make of the syrup, discharged her and sent an officer for the proprietor.
THE HARBOR.—Two schooners in from Savannah with turpentine and rosin. The rosin is for the trade; the turpentine, it is said, is for the remedies.
CITY HALL.—The Aldermen met for eleven minutes and voted themselves a dinner. The question of the street-cleaning contract was referred to the dinner.
A CARD.—Prof. Lacour, the celebrated mesmerist, is obliged to postpone his lectures at Cooper Union, having been unable to wake his assistant.

standing.text: THE SEASON.—Oysters are in, and so are the complaints. Physicians report a brisk trade in stomachs; druggists report the same.
SPORTING.—The Metropolitans beat the Brooklyns by eleven runs to four. The Brooklyns' pitcher had taken a tonic for his arm, and is said to have pitched with great confidence in the wrong direction.

standing: LOST.—A pocketbook, in a Third Avenue car, containing a pawn ticket and a prescription. The prescription is of no value to the finder.
WANTED.—A lady of refinement to sign letters of thanks for a remedy. No experience of the remedy required.
TO LET.—Two rooms over a druggist's. The smell, the landlord says, is wholesome.
POLICE COURT.—A peddler of 'Vital Bitters' was fined for obstructing the sidewalk with a crowd. The court did not inquire into the bitters, and sent out for a bottle.
FIRE.—A blaze in a tenement in Baxter street was put out by the engine company before the third floor caught. A quantity of patent medicine in a rear room burned with a blue flame for an hour.

standing.text: THE WEATHER.—Hot and close. The Health Department urges the poor to keep out of the sun, and the rich to keep out of the city, which they have.

standing: AMUSEMENTS.—At the Bowery dime museum, the Living Skeleton is to wed the Fat Lady on Thursday. The bride attributes her figure to a remedy; the groom attributes his to another.

standing.text: SHIPPING.—Cleared, the steamer Germanic for Liverpool, with grain, cotton and forty cases of an American remedy for the English market, which is said to be in need of it.

standing: A CARD.—The undersigned has not been cured by any remedy whatever, and wishes it known, having been asked eleven times this week.
WANTED.—A man with a good beard to stand in a window and be pointed at. Apply to the proprietor of a hair restorer.
THE COURTS.—A suit by a customer against a proprietor of bitters, on the ground that they contained no bitters, was dismissed. The Judge found that nobody had expected them to.

FOUND.—On the steps of a church in Mott street, a basket of two dozen bottles of soothing syrup, left by a proprietor in hope of the Sexton's endorsement. The Sexton has given it to the Board of Health.
STREET SCENE.—A sandwich man advertising a cure for consumption was taken ill at the corner of Canal street and carried home coughing, still advertising.
MARKETS.—Butter firm, eggs easier, coal dear. Patent medicines, as always, cheaper to make than to buy.
SPORTING.—At this office, a challenge: any man in the Sixth Ward may try the dumb-bells for a purse of five dollars. The purse has not been touched since Easter.
THE ELEVATED.—A gentleman fell asleep on the Second Avenue line and rode it six times. He is said to have been taking something for his nerves.
BOARDING.—Table board for gentlemen, two dollars a week. Medicines not provided at table.
CHARITY.—The ladies of St. Bartholomew's held a fair for the poor of the Sixth Ward. The poor were not admitted, but are said to have done well out of it.
WANTED.—Bottles, half-pint, round, green, by the gross. A good price for any that have been washed.
THE COURTS.—A druggist sued by a widow was found not liable, the jury holding that her husband had read the label and should have known better. The label said 'harmless.'

standing.text: THE BRIDGE.—Twenty thousand crossed the Brooklyn Bridge on Sunday. A hawker of a cure for vertigo did a good trade at the middle.
THE PARK.—Skating on the lake in Central Park; the red ball is up. A vendor of a chest balm sold out by three o'clock, chiefly to those who had watched.
CONEY ISLAND.—Forty thousand went down by the boats on Sunday. A remedy for sea-sickness was sold on the way out and a remedy for sunstroke on the way back, by the same man.
THE ICE.—The ice companies announce a short crop and a long price. Tenement mothers are advised to keep the milk in the coolest place available, which is the druggist's.

COAL.—Coal is up a dollar the ton, and the dealers say it is the weather, the railroads and the strike, in rotation. The druggists, who sell the remedy for the chill that follows, have not put up their prices, which were up already.

THE CITY.—The Board of Health reports the summer complaint among infants in the tenements, and asks mothers not to dose them with anything that makes them quiet. The druggists ask what else is for sale.
SPORTING.—The Giants have signed a pitcher from Troy. His arm is said to be made of iron; his manager has been asked to make no further claims of that kind for it.
THE SEASON.—Oysters are out until September. The fish market is quiet, and so are the stomachs; physicians are taking the opportunity to go to Saratoga.
THE WEATHER.—Snow in the night, and the streets not cleaned. The Aldermen have voted the street-cleaners a holiday, as being the most economical course.
THE WEATHER.—Rain all week. Rheumatics are reported very low; a liniment on Canal street is selling at the rate of a bottle a knee.

standing: POLICE COURT.—A man who sold a cure for baldness from a cart in Grand street was found to be bald, and was fined for misrepresentation. He has appealed, on the ground that he never claimed to use it.
THE COURTS.—A jury in the Tombs could not agree whether a tonic of forty per cent spirit was a medicine or a drink. They retired to consider it, and the bailiff reports they are still considering it.

standing.text: SHIPPING.—Arrived, the bark Celestine, from Smyrna, with figs, carpets and a quantity of opium. The figs were inspected.

standing: THE ELEVATED.—A lady on the Sixth Avenue line was relieved of her purse, her hat-pin and her opinion of the Company, in that order.
AMUSEMENTS.—At Tony Pastor's, a new comedian who imitates a patent-medicine lecture so well that two of the audience bought bottles at the door.
A CARD.—The firm of Hobart & Co. begs to inform the trade that its laudanum is unchanged in strength, and that any stronger laudanum on the street is not theirs, and is not cheaper.

standing.text: THE PULPIT.—The Rev. Dr. Parkhurst preached on the sins of the city, naming forty. Patent medicines were thirty-ninth, between the policy shops and the Elevated.

standing: CHARITY.—The Children's Aid Society asks for shoes for the newsboys. A proprietor of bitters has sent a gross of bottles instead, with his compliments.

standing.text: THE CITY.—The Brooklyn Board of Health has seized forty barrels of swill milk. The milkman says the cows were taking a tonic and are much improved.

standing: STREET SCENE.—Two rival doctors' wagons met on the Bowery and their lecturers argued for an hour, each pointing to the other's customers as evidence.
FIRE.—A blaze at a druggist's on Division street was put out with the stock, which proved more flammable than the shop. The proprietor is uninsured and unhurt, and has removed to Brooklyn.
LOST.—A small dog, answers to Dandy, last seen near a druggist's back door licking a bottle. Owner fears the worst, or the best.

standing.text: THE MARKETS.—Quinine higher on the news from Panama; camphor steady; laudanum unchanged and in good supply. Opinions on the weather are plentiful and cheap.

standing: BOARDING.—Rooms for respectable mechanics, a dollar a week. The landlady doctors free of charge and requests that boarders do not.
THE SCHOOLS.—The truant officer reports two hundred boys of the Sixth Ward in no school. Most were found selling newspapers and one was found selling a remedy, at a profit.
POLICE COURT.—A widow charged a tonic man with breach of promise, the promise being printed on the label. The court read the label and dismissed the case for vagueness.
THE DOCKS.—A longshoreman lifted a bale of cotton with one hand on a wager, then fell asleep on it. He credits a tonic for the first and his wife for the second.

standing.text: THE WHEEL.—Two hundred bicycles passed along the Boulevard on Sunday. A druggist at 59th street sells a liniment for the wheelman's knee, and another for the pedestrian's.
THE TROLLEY.—The new electric cars in Brooklyn have killed another dog and frightened a horse into the Gowanus. A tonic for the nerves of passengers is advertised on every car.
THE TELEPHONE.—A druggist on Grand street has had the telephone put in, and a customer rang him at midnight to ask for a remedy for sleeplessness. He recommended hanging up.
TAMMANY.—The Leader of the Hall has promised clean streets, clean water and a clean election. The druggists of the ward are not alarmed.

THE NEW PHOTOGRAPHY.—A physician on Second avenue now photographs the bones of his patients by the Roentgen rays, and charges extra for the photograph. Several patients have asked to be photographed thinner.
THE STRIKE.—The garment workers of the East Side are out again. The druggists report a brisk trade in remedies for the cough, which is the trade's own.
THE FLATIRON.—The new building at Madison square is twenty stories high, and the wind at its corner lifts the skirts of the ladies. Loafers gather; the police move them on.
LUNA PARK.—The new pleasure ground at Coney Island is lit by a quarter of a million electric lamps. A remedy for the eyes is sold at the gate.
THE MOTOR-CAR.—A motor-car ran down a peddler of soothing syrup on Fifth avenue. Both are said to be recovering, the syrup more quickly.
THE WAR.—Recruits for Cuba drill in the armory on Lexington avenue. The surgeons report that most of them have been taking something for the climate since April, and some of it was bitters.
THE CONSOLIDATION.—Brooklyn is now part of the city, and its druggists are learning to charge Manhattan prices.

THE MOVING PICTURES.—At Koster & Bial's the vitascope shows the surf breaking at Dover, so like the sea that the front rows drew in their feet. A lady fainted and was revived with a patent restorative sold, by coincidence, in the lobby.

standing: THE PUSHCARTS.—The pushcart men of Hester street were moved on by the police three times on Friday and were back each time before the officer. A peddler of a cough syrup among them is said to have sold the officer a bottle on the second round.

AN ORGAN-GRINDER.—An organ-grinder of Elizabeth street was fined for playing the same tune for six hours under one window. He pleaded that it was the only tune the organ knew; the court observed that the same could be said of most patent-medicine lecturers.

THE FREE LUNCH.—A saloon-keeper of the Bowery has taken the pickled eggs off his free lunch, saying the customers ate them. A druggist across the way has put out a remedy for indigestion instead, and reports a steady trade from the saloon.

THE LODGING HOUSES.—A seven-cent lodging house in the Bowery advertises a clean bed, a locker and a spoonful of tonic at bedtime. The tonic is said to account for the quiet of the house, and the locker for the lodgers' hopes.

THE ASH BARRELS.—The Street Cleaning Department reports that the ash barrels of the Sixth Ward contain, besides ashes, a great many empty bottles, most of them green and every one of them claiming to cure something.

A RUNAWAY.—A truck horse ran away in Canal street on Tuesday and was stopped by a druggist's sign, which it carried two blocks. The horse is unhurt. The sign, which promised strength, has been taken down.

THE DEAD HORSE.—A dead horse has lain in Mott street since Monday. The Street Cleaning Department says it is the contractor's; the contractor says it is the city's; the horse has ceased to take sides.

THE POLICY SHOPS.—The police raided a policy shop in Baxter street fitted up as a cigar store with no cigars. The druggist's next door is fitted up as a druggist's with no drugs to speak of, but no law against that has yet been found.

PAWNBROKERS.—The pawnbrokers of the Bowery report overcoats coming in and remedies going out. A pawnbroker of Chatham square has refused a bottle of a celebrated cordial offered as security, observing that the bottle was worth more empty.

standing.text: THE CHOWDER PARTY.—The district leader's chowder party went down the Sound on Thursday, eleven hundred voters and a barge of chowder. A tonic for the stomach was handed round on the way back, with the leader's compliments and a card for November.

THE SUNDAY SCHOOL.—The children of a mission in Rivington street went up the Hudson on their excursion, each with a flag, a bag of candy and a tract. A druggist of the street sent a bottle for the mothers; the mothers sent it back.
THE CIRCUS.—The circus is at the Garden, with three rings and an elephant said to take a tonic for its trunk. The proprietor of the tonic has asked the elephant for a testimonial, and been answered.

MOTT STREET.—The Chinese New Year was kept in Mott street with firecrackers, lilies and calls of ceremony. The merchants paid their debts before it, as is their custom; the druggists of Mulberry street, who keep no such custom, sent round their bills anyway.

standing: A WEDDING.—At a wedding in Ludlow street on Sunday the guests numbered three hundred and the chairs forty. A druggist was among the guests, and left early, with orders.
THE DISPENSARY.—The free dispensary treated four hundred on Tuesday and turned away two hundred more. The druggists of the ward are said to have treated most of the two hundred, and charged them.

THE AMBULANCE.—The hospital ambulance was called to Mulberry street three times on Saturday: once for a man hurt, once for a man drunk, and once for a man who had taken a remedy and could not say which he was.
A CARD.—Mr. J. Kessel, barber, of Grand street, wishes it known that the hair restorer in his window is for sale and not for use, and that he does not use it himself, as his customers may see.

A CARD.—The proprietors of Dr. Grimsby's Galvanic Belt regret that a wearer was struck by lightning in Jersey City. They point out that the Belt is guaranteed only against nervous debility, and that the gentleman's nerves are now perfectly quiet.
A CARD.—Mrs. Prudence Whittle thanks the ladies of New-York for their many letters, and assures them that each will have her personal attention as soon as the clerks have read it.
THE TRADE.—A wholesale druggist of Pearl street reports that the sale of empty bottles embossed CURE has doubled this year, and of bottles embossed nothing, fallen off.
THE TRADE.—A label printer of Ann street keeps six hundred testimonials in standing type, and will set any of them under any name at a dollar the hundred. Signatures extra.
THE TRADE.—The almanac of a celebrated bitters gives the weather for every day of the year, and has so far been right on Sundays.

THE COURTS.—A proprietor was sued for a cure that did not cure. His counsel showed that the plaintiff had read only the first line of the label, and the jury found for the proprietor, nobody having ever read the second.
THE COURTS.—A physician sued a druggist for refilling a prescription forty times. The druggist said the customer had asked for it, and the customer, who was in court, asked for it again.
THE COURTS.—A landlord sued a tenant for the smell of a remedy brewed in the rear room. The jury visited the premises, and returned a verdict for the tenant and an order for six bottles.
LOST.—A pair of gold spectacles, in a Grand street car, by a gentleman who cannot read the advertisements without them, and has been spared a good deal.
FOUND.—A false beard, gray, in a doorway on the Bowery, near where a medicine wagon stood. The lecturer is clean-shaven this week and twenty years younger, and has put up his price.

THE SCHOOLS.—A teacher of the Mott street school reports her class unusually quiet after the dinner hour. Inquiry shows that the mothers give the children a spoonful of a soothing syrup with their bread, on the advice of the label. The teacher has written to the label.
THE WATER.—The Croton runs brown again in the Sixth Ward. The Health Department pronounces it wholesome, and a druggist of Mott street sells a remedy for those who believe the Health Department.

STREET SCENE.—A medicine wagon in Chatham square drew two hundred with a banjo and an Indian, and sold forty bottles. The Indian is from Hoboken and the banjo from a pawnshop; the bottles are from a cellar in Mott street.

THE TENEMENTS.—The sanitary police counted eleven persons in two rooms in Baxter street, and a druggist's bottle on every shelf. The persons are to be reduced to the legal number; the bottles are not regulated.

standing.text: CHARITY.—The Association for Improving the Condition of the Poor has opened its winter rooms. Applicants are asked their names, their wages and their habits, and some are asked to leave the bottle at the door.
THE SEASON.—Strawberries are in from Delaware at ten cents the quart, and the cholera morbus at no charge. The druggists have laid in for both.
THE HEAT.—Eleven horses fell in the streets on Wednesday from the heat, and four men. The men were given a remedy at the nearest druggist's, and some of them say it was the worse of the two.

THE ROOFS.—The tenement roofs were full of sleepers on Saturday night, the rooms below being past bearing. A child rolled from a roof in Cherry street and was caught by a clothes-line, unhurt. A druggist of the street called with a soothing syrup for the fright, and was sent down the stairs again; the neighbors have given the clothes-line a vote of thanks.
THE ICE MAN.—The ice man of Elizabeth street charges a cent more the piece and delivers it smaller. He says the ice melts on the stairs; the tenants, that it melts in his wagon.

standing: THE BOWERY.—A Bowery museum exhibits a man who has taken every remedy advertised in the city and is still living. He is shown at ten cents, and is said to be the only one.

AMUSEMENTS.—A ventriloquist at a Bowery music hall makes a bottle of bitters praise itself in a loud voice. The bitters' proprietor has asked for the act to be stopped, the bottle being more convincing than he is.

THE BAND.—A German band plays in Hester street on Saturdays for coppers, and for a nickel will play something else. A druggist paid it a dollar to stand outside a rival's door and play the Dead March.

THE FERRY.—A passenger on the Fulton ferry fell overboard and was pulled out with a boat-hook, very cold and still holding a bottle of a celebrated cordial. He says the cordial kept him up; the deckhand, that he did.

standing.text: THE MARKETS.—Washington Market reports turkeys high, cranberries higher, and a remedy for dyspepsia, at the stall by the door, highest of all.

standing: BOARDING.—A widow of Second avenue offers board, a quiet house and a spoonful of a remedy at bedtime, free. Her boarders are said to be the quietest on the avenue.
THE ELEVATED.—A conductor on the Ninth Avenue line has been suspended for selling a remedy between stations. He says it was for the passengers' nerves; the Company, that it was not on the timetable.
THE TELEGRAPH.—A messenger boy took four hours to carry a message from the Battery to Union square, having stopped in Chatham square for a remedy for weak legs. He says it is slow to act.
THE ALDERMEN.—An Alderman proposed to forbid the sale of remedies on Sundays. The motion was laid over until the Alderman could be told which remedies, and by whom.
CITY HALL.—The Board of Estimate has voted the Health Department eleven new inspectors and no money to pay them. The inspectors are expected to be paid by the trade, as usual.
THE TOMBS.—A prisoner in the Tombs asked for his tonic, saying he cannot sleep without it. The Warden refused, saying that nobody in the Tombs can sleep, and that it would be unfair to the others.

BLACKWELL'S ISLAND.—The workhouse on the Island took in forty-one for drunkenness this week, eleven of whom say they had taken nothing but a tonic. The keeper has asked for the names of the tonics, and so have the other thirty.

THE PHYSICIANS.—The County Medical Society has resolved, for the eleventh year running, that patent medicines are a danger to the public. The resolution was carried unanimously, and the Society adjourned to a dinner advertised in the same columns as the medicines.

THE PHARMACISTS.—The College of Pharmacy has graduated forty young men, every one of whom can tell morphine from quinine by the taste. Several have already been offered situations by proprietors who would rather they could not.
LOST.—A green umbrella, near the Bowery, by a gentleman on his way to buy a remedy for rheumatism. He reports that the rain has since cured him of the umbrella.
A CARD.—A druggist of Grand street begs to inform the ward that he does not keep the remedy of his neighbor, will not order it, and would not sell it to his mother-in-law. It may be had next door.
FOR THE LADIES.—A remedy is advertised to restore the complexion in ten days, and another to remove the first remedy in five. Both are sold at the same counter, by the same young man.

THE BIRDS.—A bird-fancier of the Bowery sells canaries that sing, he says, because he gives them a tonic. Several customers have bought the tonic and no canary, and report that they sing a little themselves.
STREET SCENE.—A boy sold a druggist's handbills back to the druggist on Tuesday, having gathered them from the gutter. The druggist paid a cent the dozen and has had them given out again.
A FAITH CURE.—A faith healer in a hall on Second avenue cured eleven of rheumatism on Sunday, and sold them a liniment at the door, to make sure.

A PHRENOLOGIST.—A phrenologist of Broadway has read the head of a patent-medicine proprietor and found the bump of benevolence very large. The proprietor has had the chart framed, and the phrenologist has had a case of the remedy.

standing.text: THE ICE CREAM.—Eleven persons were made ill by ice cream from a cart in Orchard street. The Health Department seized the cart, and a druggist of the street sold eleven bottles.

standing: THE SODA FOUNTAIN.—A druggist of Grand street has put in a marble soda fountain with forty syrups, one of which, he says, is a remedy. The customers are invited to guess which.
TO LET.—A store, suitable for any business but medicine, the last three tenants having been in that line, and the landlord having had enough of the talk.

THE HORSE CARS.—A Third Avenue car horse lay down in the track at Grand street on Monday and could not be got up for an hour. A druggist brought out a bottle; the driver says it was the bottle that got the horse up, and the horse, which had smelled it, did not deny it.

THE MISSIONS.—A mission in the Bowery offers a bed and a sermon to any man who will sign the pledge. Several who signed are reported to have asked whether the pledge covers bitters, and been told that it does.
THE BARBERS.—The barbers of the ward have resolved to sell no hair restorer that does not restore hair. The resolution leaves them nothing to sell but shaves, and is expected to be rescinded.

THE BANK.—A savings bank of the Bowery reports deposits up in the ward this year. A proprietor of remedies on Mulberry street reports his up also, and considers that he and the bank have the same customers at different hours.
THE STOOP.—A woman of Mott street who sits on her stoop every evening reports that she has seen every remedy in the ward go past, and its customers after it, and declines to say which went faster.

A COMPLAINT.—The tenants of a house in Elizabeth street complain to the Board of Health of the smell from a druggist's cellar. The druggist complains of the smell from the tenants' cellar. The Board has sent an inspector to smell both.
THE STREETS.—A gang of the Street Cleaning Department swept Mulberry street on Wednesday, the first time since the election. The ward turned out to watch, and a druggist sold a remedy for the dust.
THE THIEVES.—A sneak thief who entered a druggist's in Canal street on Sunday night took the cash drawer and left the remedies. The druggist says the thief knew his business.
THE PEDDLERS.—A peddler of corn salve was arrested in Grand street for selling without a license, and asked the court to examine his feet. The court declined, and so did the officer.

A REUNION.—The survivors of a regiment met at a hall on the Bowery on Saturday, fewer than last year, and drank to the absent. A druggist sent a case of a tonic 'for the veterans,' who sent it on to the absent.
THE PAINTERS.—A sign painter of Canal street has painted the word CURE eleven hundred times this year, he says, and has never once been asked to paint the word WHAT.
THE CEMETERIES.—The Board of Health reports Potter's Field full, and asks for a new one. The druggists of the ward, asked for their views, had none they cared to give.

FIRE.—A blaze in a feather store in Division street was put out before the feathers went, and a druggist next door sent round a remedy for the firemen's eyes. The firemen sent round the bill for his chimney.

THE ENGINE COMPANY.—The engine company of Elizabeth street was called out three times this week, twice for fires and once for a druggist's cellar, where something had boiled over that the Chief declined to name.
MARKETS.—Coffee easier, sugar steady, cod-liver oil dear and plentiful. The children of the ward are said to hold the same view of the last.

A SOCIETY.—The Ladies' Temperance League has passed a resolution against bitters, tonics and cordials. Several members, on being shown the labels in their own cupboards, have asked for the resolution to be read again more slowly.
THE SPELLING.—A proprietor of Mulberry street has had his label set in type spelling RHUEMATISM. He says that customers who can spell are not his customers.

standing.text: THE STEAMBOATS.—The Sunday boats to Rockaway carried eleven thousand. A remedy for sunburn was sold on the boat going out and a remedy for the remedy on the boat coming back.

THE CROTON.—The water is low in the reservoirs and the Department asks the city to be sparing. The druggists of the ward, who sell nothing made without water but ask more for it, are being very sparing.

standing: A SERMON.—A preacher of Rivington street took for his text the patent medicine, and held up a bottle from the pulpit. The congregation, it is reported, chiefly wished to know where it could be had.
THE MILK.—The milk inspectors found water in the milk of eleven dealers in the ward, and chalk in two. The dealers say the milk has been taking a tonic for its color.
THE POST OFFICE.—The Post Office reports eleven hundred letters a week addressed to a Mrs. Whittle, and has asked her proprietors to call for them more often, the sack having burst.
BOARDING.—A gentleman lodger in Second avenue wishes to change his room, the room next door being taken by a man who practises the cornet, and the one above by a man who practises remedies.

standing.text: CASTLE GARDEN.—Eleven hundred landed at Castle Garden on Tuesday. Runners for the boarding-houses, the railroads and a patent pill met them at the gate, and the pill did best.
THE BOODLE ALDERMEN.—Another of the Aldermen who sold the Broadway railroad its franchise has gone to Canada for his health. The druggists of Montreal report a run on remedies for homesickness.

THE BROADWAY CARS.—The new horse cars are running on Broadway, and a gentleman who rode the stages for twenty years says the cars shake his liver loose. A druggist at Fulton street has a remedy for it.

THE OBELISK.—Cleopatra's Needle in Central Park is said to be crumbling in the climate of New-York, and learned men are to coat it with wax. A proprietor of a liniment has offered to rub it down instead.
THE AQUEDUCT.—The new Croton aqueduct is to bring the city millions of gallons more a day. The druggists, who sell a remedy for the effects of the old water, are confident of the new.
THE ELECTRIC LIGHT.—The arc lamps on Broadway hiss all night, and the moths come down from Harlem to look at them. A druggist of Union square sells a remedy for the eyes of those who look too long.

THE HIGH WHEEL.—A gentleman on a high wheel came down the Boulevard on Sunday faster than the horses, and over the handle-bar at Seventy-second street. A druggist at the corner dressed his head and sold him a liniment for the rest.

THE WILD WEST.—Colonel Cody's Wild West is at Erastina, Staten Island, with Indians, buffalo and a stage-coach robbed twice daily. A lecturer for an 'Indian' remedy who went to see it is said to have been asked by the Indians where he got it.

THE GRANT MONUMENT.—The fund for the General's tomb at Riverside is still a long way short. A proprietor of bitters has offered to make up the difference if the tomb may carry his name somewhere small.

THE ELEVATED.—The engine of a Third Avenue train showered Chatham square with live cinders on Tuesday. The ladies below complain of their bonnets, and a druggist of the square sells a remedy for their eyes.

THE STAGES.—A Broadway stage-driver, put out of work by the new cars, has taken up the selling of a remedy from the box of his old stage. He says the work is the same: shouting at people who do not want to go where he is going.

THE PEDESTRIANS.—A walking match for the championship of America is being got up at the Garden. The druggists of the city have been asked for liniment, and the backers for a doctor who will say nothing.

THE SIGNAL SERVICE.—The flag on the Equitable building flew white for fair on Wednesday and it rained all afternoon. A druggist of Broadway who had laid in umbrellas on the strength of his rheumatism did better than the Government.

THE MAYOR.—The Mayor's men have cut down the telegraph poles on Broadway and the wires are to go underground. A druggist of Canal street, whose sign hung from a pole, has gone underground with them, to a cellar.

THE GRIP.—The Russian influenza has reached the city, and every druggist has a remedy for it, most of them last winter's remedy with a new label. Physicians recommend bed, and the proprietors a bottle to take there.

A CARD.—The undersigned, having read in this paper that the type-writer will soon replace the pen, wishes to know whether it will also replace the clerk, and if so, who will buy the remedy for nerves.
THE WEATHER.—The Weather Bureau predicts fair and colder. Druggists report the colder part already selling well.
THE PULPIT.—A clergyman of Fifth avenue preached on the sins of the city, naming forty. Patent medicines were thirty-ninth, between the policy shops and the Elevated.
SPORTING.—The six-day bicycle race at the Garden enters its fifth day. The leader attributes his endurance to cold water and a clear conscience, and is not expected to win.
ELLIS ISLAND.—Fourteen hundred passed through the new station on Ellis Island on Tuesday. The doctors there look each in the eye and down the throat; the runners at the Battery look at what is left.
THE BARGE OFFICE.—The station on Ellis Island having burned, the steerage is landed at the Barge Office again, and the runners have taken their old places at the door with their handbills.

THE CABLE CARS.—The cable on Broadway runs the cars at a steady clip, and round the curve at Union square at the same clip. A druggist at the corner of Fourteenth street keeps a stock of arnica for the curve.

THE BICYCLE FACE.—A physician warns that ladies who ride the wheel develop the 'bicycle face,' a look of strain and determination. A remedy for it is advertised on Sixth avenue, and another, for their husbands, on Seventh.
THE SCORCHERS.—The bicycle squad of the police arrested eleven scorchers on the Boulevard on Sunday. One said he had taken a tonic before starting, and was fined for that too.

BLOOMERS.—A lady rode down Fifth avenue in bloomers on Saturday, followed by forty boys and a policeman. The boys were sent home. The policeman, who says he was escorting her, has been sent to Staten Island.
THE WHITE WINGS.—Colonel Waring's sweepers in their white suits have cleaned Mulberry street, and the ward does not know itself. A druggist has put up a card: REMEDIES FOR THOSE UNUSED TO FRESH AIR.

THE RAINES LAW.—A saloon in Elizabeth street has become a hotel by the addition of ten bedrooms and a sandwich. The sandwich has been served with every drink since April, and is understood to be the same sandwich.

THE RAINES LAW.—The druggists of the ward report that, the hotels having the Sunday trade in liquor, the Sunday trade in tonics has fallen off. Several have applied for a license as hotels, and are looking for a sandwich.
SUNDAY CLOSING.—The saloons being shut on Sunday by order of the Police Board, the druggists of the ward report a brisk Sunday trade in tonics, which are not liquor, and are served in a glass.
THE LEXOW COMMITTEE.—A police captain told the Senate committee that he had saved a fortune on a captain's pay by economy. The druggists of his precinct are said to have contributed to the economy.
THE BEND.—The houses of Mulberry Bend are coming down for a park, and the tenants are moving to the next street, which is now called the Bend. The druggists have moved with them.

THE PARK AT THE BEND.—The new park where Mulberry Bend stood has grass, benches and a sign forbidding everything. The old tenants come to look at it, and a druggist of Baxter street sells them a remedy for the change of air.

THE YELLOW KID.—The Yellow Kid of the Sunday colored supplement has been drawn holding a bottle. The bottle's proprietor says it is the only testimonial he has had from Hogan's Alley, and the only one in a nightshirt.
THE YELLOW JOURNALS.—The World and the Journal have each sent forty correspondents to Cuba, and a remedy for sea-sickness advertises in both, the only matter on which the two papers agree.

THE KLONDIKE.—Eleven men of the ward have started for the Klondike with picks, blankets and a remedy for the cold, guaranteed. The proprietor of the remedy has not gone himself, the gold being in the bottle.

THE ARMY BEEF.—The soldiers say the beef sent to Cuba was preserved with chemicals, and the packers that it was preserved with care. The trade of remedies, which knows something of preserving, offers no opinion.

THE WORLD'S FAIR.—Excursions leave the Grand Central daily for the Fair at Chicago. A proprietor of the ward has sent his remedy for exhibition, and the management has placed it near the Egyptian mummies.

COXEY'S ARMY.—The army of the unemployed is marching on Washington, and a druggist in Maryland has sold it a liniment for the feet. The army means to petition Congress; the druggist calls it the best trade he has had all year.

THE RING.—Under the new law a glove contest is lawful at an athletic club if it is called an exhibition. An exhibition in Brooklyn lasted twenty rounds and two physicians, and a remedy for bruises was exhibited between the rounds.

THE WALDORF.—The new hotel on Fifth avenue has a thousand rooms and a palm garden, and charges for a dinner what the ward spends on medicine in a year. Several proprietors of remedies are said to dine there.

THE PHONOGRAPH.—A phonograph parlor on Fourteenth street plays the speech of a celebrated lecturer on remedies at a nickel the hearing. It is said to be more persuasive than the lecturer, having no breath.
THE SAFETY.—A tailor of Ludlow street has bought a safety bicycle on the installment plan and rides it to the shop at seven. His landlord has put up the rent, saying he can evidently afford it.

THE WHEEL.—Eleven bicycle shops have opened on the Boulevard this year, and two livery stables have closed. A druggist at Sixty-sixth street sells a liniment for the wheel and another for the rider, and admits they are the same.

THE VOLUNTEERS.—The Seventy-first marched down Broadway for the war, every man with a bottle of a tonic 'for the climate' sent by a proprietor, who has asked the Colonel for a testimonial to be signed at the front.
THE HALF-TONES.—The papers now print photographs, and a proprietor of a hair restorer has had his before and after printed side by side. The after, his rivals say, is a photograph of his brother.
THE BRIDGE.—A man leaped from the Brooklyn Bridge on a wager on Sunday and came up alive. He says a tonic kept him afloat; the tonic's proprietor, who was on the Bridge with a placard, says the same.

THE TROLLEY DODGERS.—A gentleman of Brooklyn who has dodged the trolley cars for a year was struck by a bicycle on Sunday. The druggists of Fulton street sold him a liniment for the bicycle and a tonic for the trolley.
THE TOUR.—A proprietor of the ward has gone to Europe on the proceeds of his remedy, to study, he says, the methods of the Continent. His customers remain to study the methods of the remedy.

THE GOLD CURE.—The new institutes promise to cure the drink habit with injections of gold. Several of their patients are said to have been cured of their gold, and are now on the remedies of the ward.

THE SUBWAY DIGGINGS.—The contractors have opened Elm street from end to end, and the ward walks to work on planks. A druggist whose door now stands eleven feet above the street has put up a ladder and a card: THE REMEDY IS WORTH THE CLIMB.

THE SUBWAY.—The express carries its thousands an hour under Fourth avenue and comes up in Harlem in a quarter of an hour. Physicians warn of the bad air below; a tonic for it is sold at the head of every stair.
THE SUBWAY.—The crush at the Brooklyn Bridge station at six o'clock is such that the guards pack the passengers in with their knees. A remedy for the ribs is advertised on the platform.

THE ELECTRIC ELEVATED.—The elevated trains now run by electricity, and the cinders no longer fall on Third avenue. The ladies below have new bonnets, and the druggist of the corner no complaints of the eyes.

THE AUTOMOBILE.—A red automobile went up Fifth avenue at twenty miles an hour on Sunday, with a gentleman in goggles and a duster who did not stop to see what he had done. The druggists of the avenue report a call for remedies for the nerves of pedestrians.

THE AUTOMOBILISTS.—The Automobile Club has asked the Aldermen for better roads. The Aldermen have asked the Club for better manners. A druggist has asked both for their custom, and has a remedy for each.

THE ELECTRIC CABS.—The electric hansoms of Fifth avenue are said to be silent, clean and dear. A druggist of Broadway who has hired one to deliver his remedy says it has twice been taken for a hearse.
THE WIRELESS.—Signor Marconi sends messages across the sea without wires. A proprietor of the ward proposes to send his remedy the same way, and save the bottle.
THE TENEMENT LAW.—Under the new law every room in a new tenement must have a window. The old tenements may keep their dark rooms, and their tenants, the druggists say, their remedies.

THE POISON SQUAD.—Dr. Wiley's young men at Washington eat borax at every meal for the Government, to see what it does to them. A proprietor of the ward has offered them his remedy, and Dr. Wiley has declined it as outside the experiment.

THE MAGAZINES.—The Ladies' Home Journal, which has long refused the patent medicines' advertisements, now prints what is in them. The proprietors say the Journal is not read in the Sixth Ward, which is true.
THE HIPPODROME.—The new Hippodrome on Sixth avenue seats five thousand and floods its stage for a battle at sea. A proprietor of a remedy for chills has taken a box for the season.
DREAMLAND.—Dreamland at Coney Island shows infants in incubators, weighed daily before the public. They are said to do better than the infants of Mulberry street, being kept from the soothing syrup.

THE NICKEL SHOWS.—A store on the Bowery has been fitted with chairs and a sheet, and shows moving pictures for a nickel. A druggist next door shows his remedy in the window for nothing, and draws the smaller crowd.

THE PENNY ARCADE.—A penny arcade on Fourteenth street has forty machines, of which one tells fortunes, one tries the grip and one gives out a remedy. The last is the only one that never fails to pay out.

TIMES SQUARE.—The square at Broadway and Forty-second street is to be called Times square, after the newspaper's new building. The druggists of the old Longacre will keep the old name on their labels, which nobody reads.

THE WILLIAMSBURG BRIDGE.—The new bridge to Williamsburg is open, with room for the trolleys, the wagons and the people of Delancey street, who walk across it for the air. A druggist at the Manhattan end sells a tonic for the walk back.
THE ICE TRUST.—The ice is up to twice last year's price, and the Mayor is said to hold shares in the company. Tenement mothers keep the milk in the coolest place available, which is the druggist's.
THE COAL STRIKE.—The anthracite miners are out, and coal is three times its price when it is to be had at all. The poor of the ward buy it by the pail, and a remedy for the chest by the bottle.
THE PAN-AMERICAN.—Excursions leave daily for the Exposition at Buffalo, lit at night by the power of Niagara. A proprietor of the ward has his remedy on show there, and says it, too, is lit at night.
THE FAIR AT ST. LOUIS.—A proprietor of the ward has sent his remedy to the World's Fair at St. Louis, where it has taken a bronze medal in a class of one.
THE BOERS.—A meeting at Cooper Union cheered the Boers for two hours and the British not at all. A proprietor of a remedy for sore throats was in the gallery, taking orders.
THE RADIUM.—A lecturer at Cooper Union showed a speck of radium glowing in a tube. A proprietor in the audience has since put RADIUM on his label, there being no law against the word.

THE SKYSCRAPERS.—The Park Row Building is thirty stories high, and the elevator boys call it the dizziest building in the world. A druggist on the ground floor sells a remedy for it going up and coming down.

THE SMALLPOX.—The Health Department's vaccinators go through the tenements by night and vaccinate whoever is at home. A druggist of the street sells a salve for the arm, and another, he says, against the vaccine.
THE HIGHLANDERS.—The new American League club plays on a hilltop at Washington Heights, and the ward has not yet found it. A druggist has offered a tonic for the climb.

POST CARDS.—The picture post card has taken the city, and a druggist of Grand street has had his shop printed on one. It sells at a cent and more briskly than the remedy, being cheaper and doing no harm.
THE STEEPLECHASE.—The mechanical horses at Steeplechase Park carry eleven hundred riders a day round the course. A remedy for the stomach is sold at the finish, and a second at the gate.

THE GERMS.—A professor at the Health Department has found the germ of a disease in the common drinking cup. The druggists of the ward have taken the cup off the soda fountain and put a remedy for germs in its place.

THE TELEPHONE GIRLS.—The telephone company's girls say 'Number, please' eleven thousand times a day, and are not allowed to say anything else. A remedy for the throat has been advertised to them, and they have had no way to answer.

THE MOTOR STAGES.—A motor omnibus has been tried on Fifth avenue, and the horses of the old stages are said to have watched it go by with interest. The druggists report no change in their custom, the passengers being of the same kind.

THE AUTOMOBILE.—An automobile ran down a pushcart of oranges in Hester street on Tuesday. The oranges were picked up by the ward, and the automobilist by a druggist, who sold him a remedy for the nerves and a second for the oranges.

THE STEAMBOAT LAWS.—Since the Slocum, the steamboat inspectors have condemned life preservers by the thousand on the excursion boats, the cork in many of them having turned to dust. The trade of the ward, which knows something about labels, is not surprised.

THE RACE TRACK.—The pool-rooms of the Bowery take the wire from the tracks all afternoon. A remedy for losers is sold at the door at the price of a two-dollar ticket, and is said to do about as much good.

THE VAUDEVILLE.—A vaudeville house on Fourteenth street gives a show continuous from noon till eleven. A patron who stayed the whole of it has been taken home in a cab, and a druggist's remedy for the eyes is offered at the door.

THE MILK DEPOTS.—Mr. Straus's depots give out pasteurized milk for the infants of the tenements at a cent the bottle. The druggists of the ward have taken the soothing syrup out of the window, but not out of the shop.
THE GRIP.—The grip is in the city again, and the druggists have last winter's remedy for it under this winter's label. Physicians recommend bed, and the proprietors a bottle to take there.

THE CITY.—The Health Department now seizes watered milk in Brooklyn as in Manhattan, the boroughs being one city. The milkman says the cows have been on a tonic since consolidation, and are now Greater New York cows.
THE AQUARIUM.—The new Aquarium in Castle Garden shows fishes of every kind to the public free. A druggist of the Battery sells a remedy for sea-sickness to those who come out looking pale.
THE SPRING TONICS.—The druggists of the ward have put the spring tonics in the window, the same bottles as last spring with the word SPRING on them. The ward is said to feel the difference.

standing: THE BLOOD.—Every proprietor of the ward now sells a remedy to purify the blood. Our reporter asked one what was the matter with the blood, and was told that he would know when he had bought a bottle.
THE GUARANTEE.—A proprietor of Canal street guarantees his remedy to cure or the money returned. The money has not been asked for, his customers either being cured or not being in a position to ask.
THE HERB DOCTOR.—An herb doctor of Christie street prescribes by looking at the tongue, and has been asked by the Board of Health to look at his license. He says the license is in his other coat.

THE CLAIRVOYANT.—A clairvoyant of Second avenue diagnoses by letter, at a dollar the letter. A proprietor of the ward has written to ask what she would recommend, and been told his own remedy, at the regular price.
THE DENTIST.—A painless dentist of the Bowery draws teeth to music, the band covering the patient. A druggist next door sells a remedy for the teeth that remain.
THE BEER.—The brewers of the city have raised the price of the pail, and the druggists of the ward report the sale of bitters, which are not beer, up by the same amount.

THE CORNER.—A man has stood at the corner of Grand street and the Bowery every day for a year, saying that the end of the world is at hand. A proprietor of the corner has asked him to add that a remedy is at hand also, and he has declined.

A LOST CHILD.—A child of four found wandering in Mulberry street was taken to the station house, given a peppermint by the sergeant and claimed by its mother before supper. A proprietor of the ward who called meanwhile with a bottle of soothing syrup, for the child's nerves, was shown the door, the child's nerves being the best in the station house.
THE MIDWIVES.—The Board of Health asks the midwives of the ward to register. Several have replied that they are too busy, and one that she is a druggist.
A BIRTHDAY.—A woman of Cherry street kept her hundredth birthday on Sunday and attributed her years to never having taken a patent medicine. Three proprietors have since called to offer her one.

THE BOOTBLACKS.—The bootblacks of Park Row have formed a union and raised the price of a shine to six cents. A proprietor of a remedy for tired feet has given each boy a card to hand to his customers.

THE FIRE ESCAPES.—The inspectors report the fire-escapes of Elizabeth street so crowded with bedding, plants and bottles that a fireman could not get down them. The bottles, the inspectors say, were the hardest to move.

A DOG.—A dog of Baxter street has learned to fetch its master's remedy from the druggist's with the money in a basket. The druggist says it is his best customer, and the only one who never argues the price.
THE SCALES.—A penny weighing machine has been set up at the corner of Hester street, and the ward has found that it weighs more than it thought. A proprietor of an anti-fat remedy stands beside it.
A LECTURE.—A lecturer at Cooper Union spoke for two hours on the evils of patent medicines, and was interrupted by a cough, which a proprietor in the audience at once offered to cure.

standing.text: THE LETTER CARRIERS.—The letter carriers of the ward say that the heaviest mail of the year is the almanacs of the patent medicines, which come in January and are used for kindling in February.

standing: THE GARBAGE.—The garbage scows have been held at the dock for a week by the weather, and the ward has noticed. A druggist of Catharine street sells a remedy for the smell, which he says is the smell.

THE TENEMENT FIRE.—The tenants of a house in Monroe street who were brought down the ladders in their nightclothes on Tuesday say the first thing they saved was the rent book, and the second the remedy.

THE WIDOW'S PENSION.—A widow of Oliver street has been paid her pension by the Government after eleven years of letters. The Pension Office calls it prompt; a proprietor of the ward, who has sent her his circular every week of the eleven years, calls it his best testimonial yet.

standing.text: THE TYPE-WRITER.—A young lady type-writer in a Broadway office types sixty words a minute, and the gentlemen of the office are said to come in early to watch her. A druggist of the building sells a remedy for their nerves.
THE MISSION BAND.—A Salvation Army band has been playing on the Bowery, and was pelted. The bandsmen have asked the druggists of the street to sell them nothing for the bruises, wishing to bear them.
THE STATUE.—The pedestal on Bedloe's Island rises a course of granite a week. A proprietor of bitters, who once hoped to see the lady hold his bottle, now hopes only to see her from his roof.
THE MESSENGER BOYS.—The district messenger boys of Broadway have been timed by a gentleman with a watch and found to walk a mile in forty minutes. They say they are paid by the message, not the mile.

THE HACKMEN.—The hackmen at the Grand Central Depot charge a stranger a dollar to drive him round the block to the hotel opposite. The druggist on the corner sells the stranger a remedy for the shock.
THE PENNY PAPERS.—The newsboys now cry the Journal and the World at a cent apiece and fight over the corners. A proprietor of the ward advertises in both, and buys neither.
THE BIKE SHOPS.—A druggist of Third avenue has given over his front window to bicycle lamps and his back room to liniments. He says the two trades are the same trade, a few weeks apart.
THE ROOF GARDENS.—The roof gardens of Broadway are open, with music, ices and a breeze. A druggist of Herald square sells a remedy for those who stay up late enough to need one.

THE LIGHT.—The streets of the lower wards are to have the electric light, and the gas men are said to be taking it hard. A druggist of Grand street sells a remedy for the eyes for those not used to seeing the ward clearly.
THE EXCISE BOARD.—The Excise Board has refused licenses to forty saloons of the ward. Several of the forty have taken out licenses as druggists, and are selling the same goods in smaller glasses.
THE MOTOR WAGONS.—A brewery of the East Side has put a motor wagon on the streets, and its horses have been sold to a druggist, who uses them in his advertising as 'restored by the remedy.'
THE TELEPHONE BOOTHS.—A druggist of Grand street has put a telephone booth in his shop, at a nickel the call. He reports that most callers ask the operator for the price of a rival's remedy.

THE MOVING PICTURES.—A moving picture of a patent-medicine show has been taken on the Bowery and is shown in the halls. The lecturer in it says he was not paid, and is asking for a percentage of the remedy.
THE TRUSTS.—The newspapers say there is a trust in everything from beef to ice. The proprietors of the ward, who cannot agree on the price of a cork, deny that there is a trust in remedies.

THE GRAPHOPHONE.—A druggist of Fourteenth street has a talking machine in his window that recites a testimonial every five minutes, in a voice said to be a dead man's. He says it is the same testimonial the man gave living.
THE AEROPLANE.—Two brothers in Ohio are said to have flown in a machine. A proprietor of the ward says his customers have been flying for years, and at a fraction of the cost.
THE BRONX.—The subway to the Bronx is open, and the ward has gone to look at the country. A druggist at the end of the line sells a remedy for hay fever to those who find it.

standing: THE RECIPE.—A woman of Mott street has sold her grandmother's recipe for a cough syrup to a proprietor of the ward for five dollars. The grandmother, who is living, says the recipe was for preserves.

THE TESTIMONIALS.—A proprietor of Canal street has printed a testimonial from a gentleman of Chicago who, on inquiry, lives in Hoboken and has never been to Chicago or taken the remedy. He says he would recommend it, if asked.
THE SAMPLE.—A proprietor of the ward gave away a thousand sample bottles in Hester street on Saturday. Several of the bottles have since been seen for sale in Orchard street, at five cents.

THE LABELS.—A label of a Mulberry street remedy promises relief from forty-one complaints, in type so small that a magnifying glass is given with every bottle. The glass is said to be the more useful.

THE DOSE.—A proprietor was asked by our reporter what the dose of his remedy was. He said a tablespoonful, or a wineglassful in severe cases, or the bottle in very severe cases, and that most cases are very severe.

standing.text: A PRIZE.—A proprietor of the Bowery offers a gold watch to the customer who sends in the most wrappers of his remedy by Christmas. The leader is said to have sent in two hundred, and to be very quiet.

standing: THE CANVASSERS.—Canvassers for a remedy have been going from door to door in Henry street with a book of testimonials and a sample spoon. The tenants report that the spoon is the better made.

THE DEACON.—A deacon of a church in Madison street has signed a testimonial to a bitters, saying that it is no stronger than a strong tea. The temperance ladies of the church have asked him which tea.
A COMPLAINT.—A customer of a remedy of the ward complains that a bottle bought on Monday was green and one bought on Thursday brown. The proprietor says the remedy is seasonal.
THE MARKETS.—Opium firm at the Custom House, the Smyrna crop being short. The proprietors of the ward, who are not supposed to have any interest in the matter, are watching it closely.
THE MARKETS.—Glass bottles up a cent the dozen, corks steady, labels cheap. Proprietors of remedies report the contents, as always, the least of their expenses.

THE BANK BOOK.—A proprietor of the ward has opened an account at a savings bank under another name. The bank says many proprietors do, the remedy business being one in which a man may have to change his name at short notice.
A CLERGYMAN.—A clergyman of the Bowery has refused a hundred dollars for his testimonial to a nerve tonic. The proprietor has raised his offer, and the clergyman his price.

THE ACADEMY.—The Academy of Medicine heard a paper on the patent remedies of the city, with the contents of forty bottles. The paper was not printed, several of the proprietors being subscribers to the Academy's hospital.
THE BARBERS.—A barber of Grand street sells a hair tonic of his own making, and his customers ask him why he is bald. He says that he is the before.

THE STATION HOUSE.—The sergeant at the Elizabeth street station house reports that his men took up eleven men this week who said they had taken nothing but a tonic. He has begun keeping a list of the tonics, which he says is shorter than the list of the men.
