THE LOCKSMITH.—A locksmith of Canal street was called to a druggist's on Sunday to open the cellar, the druggist having locked himself in with his stock. He was found in good spirits.
THE GOAT.—A goat of Cherry street ate the label off a bottle of a remedy left on a stoop, and is said to be better for it. The proprietor has used the goat in his advertising, without asking.
THE HAT.—A hatter of the Bowery reports that the proprietors of remedies are his best customers, each ordering a new hat after a good month and the same hat cleaned after a bad one.
THE STOVE.—A woman of Hester street who brewed a remedy of her own on the kitchen stove has been asked by the landlord to stop, and by the neighbors to sell them some.

standing.text: THE CHILDREN'S AID.—The Children's Aid Society has sent a party of the ward's orphans to farms in the West. A proprietor of a tonic has sent a case with them, for the farmers.

standing: THE LECTURE.—A lecturer at a Bowery hall showed the audience a tapeworm in a jar, and sold a remedy for it at the door. Several of the audience who had never had a tapeworm bought two bottles.
THE BOARDING-HOUSE.—A boarding-house of St. Mark's place forbids remedies at table. The boarders take them in the hall, and the landlady says the hall is now the most popular room in the house.

THE JURY.—A juror at the General Sessions asked to be excused, being a proprietor of remedies with a large mail to answer. The Judge excused him, saying the mail was probably more urgent than the case.
THE STABLES.—A veterinary of Elm street sells a liniment for horses which several hackmen have been seen to use on themselves. The veterinary says the dose is the same, and the result.

THE MAYOR'S OFFICE.—The Mayor's marshal has licensed forty new peddlers this month, eleven of them for remedies. The marshal says the remedies are the easiest to license, being the hardest to inspect.

THE PAWN TICKETS.—A pawnbroker of Division street lent a dollar on a bottle of a celebrated tonic, the owner swearing it was worth five. The bottle has not been redeemed, and the pawnbroker is drinking it to find out.
THE STOCK.—A proprietor whose shop burned in Canal street says the fire was put out by the remedy, which ran from the shelves in a flood. The fire marshal says the flood made the fire worse.
A TRIAL.—A peddler accused of selling colored water as a cure was acquitted when his counsel showed that the color was genuine.

THE MORGUE.—The Morgue reports eleven unclaimed this week, and the Department asks the public to come and look. A proprietor of the ward has sent a man to see whether any are customers, and he has reported that it is hard to say.
A REUNION.—The Old Guard of the Sixth Ward dined at a hall in Grand street, and toasted the days when the ward had no doctors, only druggists, and was healthier. The druggists present drank to that.
THE SLEEPERS.—A gentleman who fell asleep in a Bowery barber's chair after taking a remedy for his nerves was shaved, trimmed and shampooed before he woke, and refused to pay for any of it.

standing.text: THE HORSE CARS.—The horse car men of the city have struck for twelve hours a day, and walk the streets with their whips. The druggists sell them a remedy for the feet, which they say is a new experience.
THE GASLIGHT.—The gas company has raised its price, and the druggists of the ward sell more candles and more remedies for the eyes. They report the two trades a natural pair.
THE STREET CLEANERS.—The street-cleaning contractor's men swept Mott street once this month, by the calendar, and are paid for four. The druggists sell a remedy for the dust the once raised.
THE MOTOR CAR.—A druggist of upper Broadway has bought an automobile to deliver his remedy, and the remedy is said to arrive shaken up, which he says is as the label directs.
THE STRIKE.—The subway diggers struck for more pay and the streets above stayed open a week. The druggists of Elm street, whose doors had been in a trench, report the best week of the year.

THE NEW LAW.—The proprietors of the ward have begun to read the labels of their rivals' remedies, to see what will have to be declared. Several have been surprised, and one has been surprised by his own.

THE SUFFRAGISTS.—The ladies of the suffrage society held a meeting at Cooper Union and were heckled from the gallery. A proprietor of a remedy for female complaints sent a box of his pamphlets, which were returned unopened.

THE RADIUM.—A proprietor of the ward who added the word RADIUM to his label has been asked by a physician how much radium is in it. He has answered that there is as much radium in it as there is in the physician's practice.

THE BOODLE BOARD.—Another of the Aldermen who voted the Broadway franchise has gone to Canada for his health. The druggists of the City Hall district report that the climate of Montreal is now the most recommended in the city.

MR. COMSTOCK.—The Society for the Suppression of Vice has seized an almanac of a proprietor of the Bowery for a woodcut of a lady's ankle, in an advertisement for a liniment. The almanac's sale is said to have trebled since.

THE ELEVATED.—A cinder from the engine of the Third Avenue line set fire to a lady's bonnet at the Grand street station. A druggist at the foot of the stairs had a burn salve ready, and is said to stand there for the purpose.

THE WIRES.—The telegraph and telephone poles of Broadway are coming down by order of the Mayor, and the wires are to go underground. The proprietors who nailed their signs to the poles have asked the city where they are to go.

THE ELECTRIC LIGHT.—The arc lamps on Broadway are said by a physician to injure the eyes, and by the gas company to injure everything. A proprietor of an eye-water has set up his stand under the brightest one.

THE TYPEWRITER.—A young woman of the Bowery has been engaged by a proprietor to work a type-writing machine at six dollars a week. She types his testimonials, and is said to be the only one in the house who believes them.

THE CHAMPION.—Mr. Sullivan, the champion, has been advertised as taking a certain bitters before every fight. Mr. Sullivan's manager says he takes a great many things before every fight, and has asked for a share of the bitters.

THE BEND.—A police captain says there are more thieves in Mulberry Bend than in any acre of the city. The druggists of the Bend say there are more customers, and have asked that the two not be confused.
THE KNIGHTS.—The Knights of Labor met at Clarendon Hall and asked for the eight-hour day. A proprietor of a nerve tonic who works his bottle-washers twelve hours sent a case, with his good wishes.

THE HORSE DISEASE.—The horses of the car lines are down with the epizootic again, and the cars are drawn by men. A druggist of the Bowery has a remedy for the horses, and another for the men, and the same bottle serves.

THE DUDE.—A young gentleman of Fifth avenue who carries a cane and parts his hair in the middle has been taken ill on Broadway. A proprietor offered him a tonic for dudes, which he says is the first ever put up for the class.

THE STATUE.—The pieces of the Statue lie in their crates on Bedloe's Island while the pedestal waits for its last courses of granite. A proprietor of bitters has asked whether the crates are to be sold afterward, for bottles.

THE NEW AQUEDUCT.—The tunnel of the new aqueduct is dug through to Harlem, and the engineers say the city will have water enough for a million more. The proprietors of the city, who use it in their remedies, say they will try to keep up.

THE ELECTRIC CHAIR.—The State has put a murderer to death at Auburn by electricity, and the newspapers are not agreed that it was quick. A proprietor of an electric belt has withdrawn his advertisement for the week.

AROUND THE WORLD.—Miss Bly of the World is home from her trip round the globe in seventy-two days. A proprietor of the ward has put out a tonic for travelers, and says it would have done it in seventy.

THE FLOOD.—The relief fund for Johnstown has passed a hundred thousand dollars in this city. A proprietor of the ward sent a crate of his remedy to the relief train, and the railroad has asked him to send money instead.

THE TOBOGGAN.—A toboggan slide has been built in a vacant lot at Harlem, and the young people slide down it by torchlight. The druggists at the foot sell a liniment, and the druggists at the top a remedy for courage.

THE DIME MUSEUM.—A museum of the Bowery exhibits a man who has taken every patent medicine on the market, and lived. The proprietors of the city have sent their bottles to be added, and the man has asked for a raise.

CASTLE GARDEN.—The commissioners report that the runners of the boarding-houses are kept out of the Garden, and wait at the gate instead. A druggist's runner who waits with them has a handbill in eight languages, all of them advertising the same bottle.

THE BUCKET SHOP.—A bucket shop in Broad street has failed, and its customers have learned what their margins were. A proprietor of the ward who lost a hundred dollars there says he will make it back on the nerve tonic, from the other customers.

THE CORNER IN WHEAT.—The papers say a Chicago man has cornered the wheat. The bakers of the ward have put up the loaf, and a proprietor of a tonic for the appetite has taken his advertisement out until it comes down.

DR. PARKHURST.—The Reverend Dr. Parkhurst has toured the dives of the city in disguise, to see for himself, and has preached on what he saw. A druggist of the Tenderloin says he recognized him, and sold him something for his nerves.

THE YELLOW KID.—The comic picture of the boy in the yellow nightgown has the city laughing, and his face is on every kind of goods. A proprietor of the ward has put it on his label, without asking anyone, which is what the boy would have done.
THE KINETOSCOPE.—A parlor on Broadway shows moving pictures through a peep-hole at five cents the machine. A proprietor of an eye-water stands at the door as the customers come out.

THE VITASCOPE.—The moving pictures were thrown on a sheet at Koster & Bial's, and the audience ducked when the waves came in. A proprietor of the ward has asked whether a picture can be made of his remedy working.

THE KLONDIKE.—Men are leaving the city for the gold fields of the Yukon by every train, and the druggists are selling them a Klondike Outfit of quinine, liniment and bitters. The miners who come back say they found the bitters most useful, for trading.

THE BIG STORE.—The new store on Sixth avenue has a fountain, a band and a counter for everything, including remedies. The druggists of the avenue say they cannot compete, and have put up their prices to show it.

THE ANTITOXIN.—The Health Department gives the new serum for diphtheria free to the poor, and the children who have it live. The proprietors of the patent diphtheria cures have asked the Board whether this is fair competition.

THE BICYCLE.—A clergyman of the city has preached against the Sunday wheel, and his congregation has gone to the country on Sunday to think it over. A druggist of the Boulevard sells a liniment for the sermon.
THE BEND IS GONE.—The houses of Mulberry Bend are down, and there is to be a park where they stood. The druggist of the corner, whose shop still stands, says he will sell to the park.

THE NEW PARK.—The park in Mulberry Bend is open, with grass, benches and a notice to keep off the grass. The children of the ward have taken to it, and a druggist on the edge of it sells a remedy for grass stains.

THE CABLE.—The Broadway cable stopped on Tuesday for an hour with three hundred cars on it. A proprietor of a nerve tonic walked the line selling it to the passengers, and says the cable has been his best friend.

THE WALDORF.—The new hotel on Fifth avenue has a dining room in which nobody may sit in a sack coat. A proprietor of the Bowery took his remedy there to sell it, in a frock coat, and was shown the way to the tradesmen's door.

THE JOURNAL.—The new owner of the Journal has bought the whole staff of a Sunday supplement from his rival. A proprietor of the ward has asked whether he would buy a testimonial, and was told he had his own.

THE TELEPHONE.—A druggist of Grand street has put a telephone in his shop, and the ward calls the doctor from it at ten cents the call. The doctor, the druggist says, comes in about an hour, and the remedy in about a minute.

THE SILVER QUESTION.—Free silver is argued in every saloon of the ward, and nobody in the ward has any silver to free. A proprietor has put out a tonic at sixteen cents, and says it is worth a dollar in gold.

THE HARD TIMES.—The soup kitchens of the city fed more this winter than any winter since 'seventy-three. The proprietors of the tonics for the appetite have taken out their advertisements, as being in poor taste, and put them back in March.

THE BARGE OFFICE.—The steerage are landed at the Barge Office while the new station on the Island is built. A proprietor of the Battery has put up a sign in nine languages, and says it reads the same in all of them: CURES.

THE ROUGH RIDERS.—Colonel Roosevelt's regiment is home from Cuba, and a proprietor of the Bowery has put out a Rough Riders' Tonic with a picture of the charge. The Colonel's friends say it is the first charge he has not led.
THE MAINE.—A proprietor of the ward has put out a 'Remember the Maine' bitters, with a picture of the ship on the label. The Navy has asked him to remember it some other way.

THE STEREOPTICON.—Advertisements are thrown by the magic lantern on a sheet over Herald square every night. A proprietor of a cough remedy has bought a minute between the election returns, and the crowd cheered it, by mistake.

THE GOLD CURE.—An institute in Twenty-third street cures the drink habit with gold in the veins, and has a waiting room full. A proprietor of bitters has sent his card to every patient, for when they are cured.

THE MESSENGER BOYS.—The messenger boys of the city have struck for two cents more the message. A proprietor of the ward who sends his circulars by them says he will send them by post, which is slower but does not strike.
THE NEWSBOYS' STRIKE.—The newsboys will not sell the World or the Journal until the price is put back. A druggist of Park row has sold the strikers a lozenge for the voice, and says he is with them.

THE HOTTEST DAY.—A hundred horses fell dead in the streets in the heat, and the Street Cleaning Department could not take them away fast enough. The druggists of the ward sold a cooling cordial by the bucket, and the bucket is said to have been the cooler.

THE POISON SQUAD.—Dr. Wiley's young men at Washington eat borax with every meal for the Government, to see what it does. The proprietors of the city, who have been feeding it to the public for years without asking, are said to be following the inquiry.

THE SUBWAY DIGGING.—The street is up from City Hall to the Grand Central for the underground railway, and the shopkeepers say their custom has gone down the hole. A druggist on the line has put a ladder into the trench, and sells to the diggers.
THE BLAST.—A blast in the subway works blew in the windows of a block on Park avenue, and the dust settled on Murray Hill. A proprietor of an eye-water was on the corner by noon.

THE FLATIRON.—The wind at the corner of the new triangular building at Twenty-third street lifts the ladies' skirts, and the police move along the gentlemen who come to watch. A proprietor has hired a boy to stand there with his handbills, which also blow away.

THE WILLIAMSBURG BRIDGE.—The new bridge to Brooklyn is open, and the East Side can walk to Williamsburg in half an hour. The druggists of both ends report the bridge a great convenience, for selling the same bottle at two prices.
THE WIRELESS.—Signor Marconi has sent a message across the ocean without a wire. A proprietor of the ward says he has been sending cures through the air for years, by advertisement.
THE AUTO-CAB.—Electric cabs ply on Fifth avenue at a fare the hansoms cannot match. A hansom driver of the Fifth Avenue Hotel says he will hold out, and has taken a tonic to do it.
THE SPEED LAW.—The law has limited the motor cars to a speed the motor cars say they have never heard of. They have not slowed, and a druggist of the Boulevard reports the liniment trade unchanged.

MRS. NATION.—Mrs. Nation of Kansas, with her hatchet, visited the city and the saloons of the Bowery shut their doors. The druggists of the Bowery did not, and Mrs. Nation, who had not been told about them, went home.

THE NEW STATION.—The new immigrant station on Ellis Island, of brick and stone, is open. The doctors look at every eye and every chest, and a proprietor of the Battery has asked whether they will look at his remedy as well, and was told they had.

THE NICKELODEON.—A store on Fourteenth street has been fitted with chairs and a sheet, and shows moving pictures all day at five cents. A druggist next door sells a remedy for the eyes to those who come out, and a remedy for the nerves to those who go in.

THE INSURANCE INQUIRY.—Mr. Hughes has found that the great insurance companies paid the politicians out of the widows' money. A proprietor of the ward who pays his politicians out of his own says he feels very honest.

THE WAR IN THE EAST.—The Japanese have the Russians shut up in Port Arthur, and camphor is up again. The proprietors of the camphor liniments have put up their prices out of sympathy, with both sides.

THE PEACE.—The Russians and the Japanese have made peace at Portsmouth, with the President's help. A proprietor of the ward has put out a Peace Tonic, and says it is the first thing the two countries have agreed on.
THE ARCTIC.—Commander Peary has sailed again for the Pole. A proprietor of a warming cordial has sent a case, and will advertise it either way.

THE GREAT WHITE WAY.—Broadway from Madison square to Longacre is lit with electric signs, and a remedy for sleeplessness is advertised in letters of light ten feet high. The druggists of the side streets report that the sign keeps the whole block awake.

THE MOTOR BUS.—A motor omnibus is running on Fifth avenue on trial, and the passengers on the top say the view is fine and the smell is not. A proprietor has asked to put his notice on the side, and was told it would be smelled before it was read.

THE HAND CAMERA.—A young woman with a hand camera has photographed the shop windows of Grand street for an exhibition. The proprietors of the street, who usually pay for their pictures, have asked her terms.

THE TRADING STAMPS.—The stores of Grand street give green stamps with every purchase, to be pasted in a book and exchanged for a lamp. A proprietor of the ward gives stamps with his remedy, and says three books will buy a second bottle.

THE GRAMOPHONE.—A machine in a Bowery parlor plays a recorded speech on the virtues of a remedy, for a cent in the slot. The proprietor says the machine is more believed than he is, and works longer hours.
THE PIANOLA.—A piano that plays itself from a roll of paper is shown in a window on Fifth avenue. A proprietor of a nerve tonic has stood his bottle on top of it, and says the music is the tonic's.
THE CENSUS.—The new census gives Greater New York three and a half millions. The proprietors of the city have reckoned the bottles to match, and found the market wanting.

THE TENEMENT LAW.—The new tenement law forbids the dark room and the school sink, and the landlords of the ward have called it confiscation. A druggist of the ward who owns two houses says he agrees with the landlords, as a landlord, and with the law, as a druggist.
THE ICE BOX.—The new ice boxes are sold on the installment plan, a dollar down and a dollar a week. The druggists of the ward, who sell the milk syrups, say the ice box is a passing fancy.

THE AEROPLANE.—A gentleman of Long Island says he will fly to Coney Island by summer in a machine of his own building. A proprietor of the ward has offered to put his name on the wings, and the gentleman has asked how much.

THE SUBWAY CROWD.—The underground cars carry four hundred thousand a day, most of them standing. The druggists at the stations sell a remedy for the feet, and another for the elbows of the other passengers.
THE PURE FOOD BILL.—The bill for pure food and drugs is before Congress again, and the proprietors of the city have gone to Washington to see the members. They say they went to see the Capitol.

THE CHEMISTS' REPORT.—A chemist of the Agricultural Department reports that a celebrated soothing syrup is one part in ten morphine. The proprietors say the chemist must have taken a spoonful himself, to report it so calmly.

standing: THE LOTTERY.—A policy shop in the back of a cigar store in Baxter street has been raided, and the slips taken for evidence. The numbers played most this week were those on the label of a celebrated remedy, which the remedy's proprietor calls a testimonial.

THE PAWNSHOP.—A pawnbroker of the Bowery reports more bottles of patent medicine pledged this month than watches. He lends a nickel on the full bottle and nothing on the empty, which he says is the only fair valuation of the trade.

THE PHYSICIAN'S SIGN.—A young physician has put up his sign in the ward, and the druggists of the street have called on him with their cards and their rates. He has asked what the rates are for, and has been told he will learn.

A CORRECTION.—The Gazette stated last week that a remedy of the Bowery contains nothing harmful. The Gazette has since learned that the remedy contains nothing at all, and is happy to correct the impression.

THE CHURCH FAIR.—The ladies of a church in Madison street held a fair for the organ fund, and a proprietor of bitters took a table. He took more than the organ fund, and has been asked to give a little of it to the organ.

THE LECTURE COURSE.—A course of lectures on hygiene has been given at the Cooper Union to large audiences. The lecturer advised plain food, fresh air and no patent medicines, and sold a pamphlet of his own at the door, at a quarter.
THE BARBER'S POLE.—A barber of Hester street who sells a hair restorer is himself perfectly bald, and says it is the proof of his honesty. His customers say it is the proof of something.

THE SPIRIT MEDIUM.—A medium of Second avenue has been asked by a widow to consult her late husband about a remedy he took. The husband, through the medium, recommended another, which the medium also sells.

THE CROSSING SWEEPER.—The crossing sweeper at Chatham square has swept the same crossing for thirty years, and says he has never had a cold. A proprietor of a cough remedy has offered him a dollar to say otherwise.
THE CLOCKMAKER.—A clockmaker of Division street has made a clock that strikes the hour for taking a remedy, and sells it to the proprietors. One of them has had it set to strike every half-hour.
THE ALMANAC.—A proprietor's almanac for the year predicts a hot summer, a cold winter and a sickly spring. The Weather Bureau has asked him how he knows, and he has sent them a copy.
THE DISPENSARY.—The dispensary in Centre street treated more than two hundred on Saturday, free. A druggist across the street, who charges, says the dispensary is ruining the ward's character.

THE COUNTERFEITER.—A man has been taken in Elizabeth street for counterfeiting the label of a celebrated remedy. The remedy's proprietor says the counterfeit was the better bottle, and wants to know who filled it.

THE SUNDAY SCHOOL.—A Sunday school of the ward gave its scholars a picture card for good attendance, and a proprietor of a tonic printed the cards. The cards carry a text on one side and the tonic on the other, and the children read the tonic.

THE FIREMEN'S BALL.—The firemen of the ward held their ball at a hall in the Bowery, and the dancing went on until four. A druggist of the street sold a remedy for the feet at the door at four, and is said to have stood there since two.
THE SCALE.—A druggist of Hester street has a penny scale that tells the weight and a card that tells the remedy. Everyone who has stood on it has been told to take the same one.

THE BLIND MAN.—A blind man who sells pencils on the Bowery has been offered five dollars by a proprietor to say that an eye-water restored his sight. He has declined, and says he would rather sell pencils, which do what they are said to.

THE SALESMAN.—A drummer for a Chicago remedy has been through the ward with a sample case, and left a dozen bottles at every druggist's on sale or return. The druggists have returned the bottles, empty, and asked for more.

THE COLLEGE.—The College of Pharmacy has graduated its class, and the young men have been engaged by the druggists of the city at eight dollars a week. They are said to know a great deal about the drugs, and to be learning the rest at the counter.
THE INQUIRY OFFICE.—A proprietor of the ward has opened an inquiry office where the afflicted may ask about their symptoms free. Every symptom yet asked about has been found to want his remedy.

THE HAIR.—A lady of Grand street whose hair turned white overnight from a fright has been offered a dye by four proprietors and a remedy for the fright by a fifth. She has taken neither, and is said to look very well.
THE DOG SHOW.—The dog show at the Garden had fourteen hundred dogs and a proprietor selling a remedy for the dogs' nerves. The dogs were not consulted; their owners were, at fifty cents.
THE STOOP.—The ward sat on its stoops on Sunday evening for the first time since October, and the druggists put their chairs out too, with a tray of remedies beside each.
THE MORTGAGE.—A druggist of the ward has bought the house over his shop with the profits of a cough remedy. The tenants say they will cough less, now they know where it goes.
THE SIGN-PAINTER.—A sign-painter of the Bowery has painted CURES on more windows this year than any other word. He says he has no opinion on the matter, and charges by the letter.
THE BEGGING LETTER.—A proprietor of the ward has received a letter from a gentleman in Ohio asking for a bottle free, for a testimonial. The proprietor has sent a testimonial free, for a bottle.
THE ORGAN.—An organ-grinder of Mulberry street plays the same tune under every window until he is paid to move. A druggist of the street pays him to stand under his rival's.

THE SPELLING BEE.—A spelling bee at a hall in Second avenue was won by a girl of twelve, who spelled 'pharmaceutical' without a pause. A proprietor in the audience has offered her a place, to write his labels, which nobody else in the trade can spell.

THE EXCURSION.—The Sunday-school excursion to Glen Island came home at dark with every child accounted for and every basket empty. A druggist of the street met the boat with a remedy for the cramps, and sold out on the pier.
THE INVENTOR.—A gentleman of Twelfth street has patented a bottle that cannot be refilled, and has offered it to the proprietors of the city. They have declined it, refilling being half the trade.

THE PEDDLER'S LICENSE.—The Mayor's marshal has taken the licenses of eleven peddlers of the Bowery for selling remedies from a cart. The druggists of the Bowery, who sell the same remedies from a shop, were not visited.

THE QUACK.—A man calling himself a professor of nerves has been arrested in Second avenue for practising without a license. His patients have come to court to testify that he cured them, and the court has asked them of what.
THE STRAW HAT.—The straw hats came out on the first warm Saturday, and the druggists' windows filled with a remedy for the sunstroke. The hats are said to be a better protection, at the same price.
THE SKATES.—The roller-skating rink on Third avenue is full every night, and a druggist of the avenue keeps a chair by his door for those who fall outside it.

A WIDOW'S CARD.—Mrs. Bridget Mulroy, of Cherry street, wishes it known that her late husband took no remedy in his last illness, whatever the label on the bottle in the window of a Bowery shop may say.

THE CHAIR.—A barber of the Bowery has a chair that tilts, rocks and plays a tune, and a druggist next door has bought one for his customers to wait in. They say they feel better already, before the remedy.
THE FALSE TEETH.—A dentist of the Bowery offers a full set for five dollars and a remedy for the gums for twenty-five cents more. The ward is said to be buying the remedy and keeping its own teeth.

THE NEWSPAPER.—A rival paper of the city has printed an article against the patent medicines on page four, and eleven advertisements for them on page five. Its editor says the two pages are under different management.

THE CANDY STORE.—A candy store of Hester street has been found selling a cough drop with chloroform in it, to children, at a cent. The Board of Health has taken the drops, and the candy store has taken a druggist's license.

THE HOTEL.—A gentleman from Chicago who stopped at a hotel on Broadway has left a trunk full of a remedy he was to introduce to the city. The hotel has introduced it to the hall porters, who say it is very like the Chicago gentleman.

standing.text: THE FIRE ESCAPE.—The fire-escapes of the ward are hung with bedding, children and bottles in the hot nights. The Fire Department asks that the escapes be kept clear, and the druggists ask nothing, having sold the bottles.
THE COLD SNAP.—The water froze in the hydrants and the ward went to the pump at the corner, which a druggist of the street has had painted with his name.

THE SNOW.—The snow was carted from Broadway to the river by night, and from Mulberry street not at all. A druggist of Mulberry street has dug out his own doorway and no one else's, which he says is enterprise.

THE SPRING CLEANING.—The housewives of the ward have the carpets out on the lines and the beaters going from dawn. A druggist of the street sells a remedy for the dust, and the dust comes in at his door for nothing.

THE BATHING.—The free floating baths are moored off the Battery and the East Side, and the boys of the ward are in them from six to dark. A proprietor of the ward who sells a soap that cures everything has had his handbills thrown in after them.

THE SCHOOL.—The schools opened on Monday with more children than seats, and the Board of Education asks for more schools. A proprietor of a tonic for the growing child has asked the Board whether it wants more bottles.
THE LEAVES.—The leaves are down in the Park and the colds are up in the ward, the druggists say, by a law of nature they have studied carefully.
THE GRIP SEASON.—The physicians say it is the grip and the druggists say it is the season, and both are selling the same remedy under different names.

THE ICE HARVEST.—The ice is a foot thick on the Hudson and the cutters are at work. The ice companies say the crop is short; the cutters say it is the longest they have seen; the price will be settled in July.

THE MOSQUITOES.—The mosquitoes of the Jersey flats have come across the river, and the ward sleeps under netting or not at all. A druggist of the street sells a lotion that the mosquitoes are said to prefer.
THE PEACHES.—Delaware peaches are in at the markets at ten cents the basket, and the cholera morbus with them. The druggists, who know the season, have the remedy in the window beside the peaches.

THE CHESTNUTS.—The chestnut men are on the corners with their roasters, and a druggist of Grand street has put a roaster by his door to draw the crowd to his window. He says the chestnuts sell better than the remedy, and cost less to make.

second_still: a second copper, which the coppersmith will let him have once two hundred bottles have gone over the counter
a second still, which the coppersmith of Elm street keeps for a man who has sold two hundred bottles
percolator: the use of a glass percolator, which the instrument maker will teach a man who has run ten batches
the percolator, a glass the trade lets a man have once he has run ten batches and shown he can be trusted with it
newspaper_ads: a notice in the Gazette, which is to be had by a man with a hundred dollars in the bank and a customer grateful in print
space in these columns, which the Gazette sells to a man with a hundred dollars put by and a testimonial in print
a notice in this paper, which the Gazette will print for a man with a hundred dollars in hand and a grateful customer in type
doctor_title: the title of Doctor, which the ward allows a man in good standing, and a college by post allows anyone with fifty dollars
being called Doctor, which the ward will do for a man of good standing, and a college by post for a fee
a doctor's title, which comes to a man the ward thinks well of, or by post to a man who sends the fee
third_still: a third copper, which the coppersmith keeps for a house that has sold six hundred bottles
a third still, which the coppersmith will put in for a house that has sold six hundred bottles
coroner_fees: an understanding with the coroner, which every proprietor comes to after his first inquest
the coroner's acquaintance, which a proprietor makes at his first inquest and keeps by calling on him before the next
an arrangement with the coroner's office, of the kind a proprietor learns of when he first sits through an inquest
quality_control: a chemist of his own, to be engaged after forty batches with a hundred dollars put by, or at once if a bad batch ever comes to light
a taster for his batches, which a house takes on after forty batches and a hundred dollars in hand, or after its first bad batch
larger_shop: the empty shop next door, the cobbler's that was, which the landlord offers at five dollars a month to a proprietor with twenty-five regulars
the empty shop next door, the cobbler's that was, which the landlord will let at five dollars a month once the shop has twenty-five regulars
bulk_supplier: terms from an importer on Pearl street, who gives them to a house that has brewed twenty-five batches
a discount from a Pearl street importer, who extends it to a house of twenty-five batches

standingDated.text: THE PEDESTAL FUND.—The World asks a dollar of every reader toward a pedestal for the Statue, which the French are taking to pieces in Paris to be crated for the voyage. A proprietor of bitters has offered a hundred dollars if the lady may hold one of his bottles instead of the torch.

GENERAL GRANT.—The General is dead at Mount McGregor, of the cancer in his throat that kept him writing his memoirs to the last. The druggists of the ward report that he took nothing for it but cocaine and a little morphine, and offer both at the usual rates.
THE FUNERAL.—The General's funeral went up Broadway for five hours. The ward is draped in black; a throat lozenge is advertised in his memory at a reduction.
THE PEDESTAL FUND.—The World's subscription has passed a hundred thousand dollars, chiefly in dimes from schoolchildren. The proprietor of bitters has withdrawn his offer and sent a dollar.
JUMBO.—Mr. Barnum's great elephant has been killed by a locomotive in Canada. The druggists of the ward, who had been selling a 'Jumbo Liniment,' have reduced the bottle.
THE PRESIDENT'S WEDDING.—The President has married Miss Folsom at the White House. A proprietor of a tonic has sent the couple a case, and advertised that he did.
THE STATUE.—Liberty is unveiled in the harbor in a fog so thick that the guns could not find her. The ward celebrated with fireworks and a remedy, and some will feel both for a week.
THE ELECTION.—Mr. Henry George, of the single tax, runs for Mayor with the workingmen behind him. A druggist of the Bowery has named a tonic for him, and taxes nothing but the bottle.
THE BLIZZARD.—Snow to the second story in Mulberry street; no cars, no coal, no milk. The druggists alone kept their doors open, and their prices.
THE ELECTION.—The ward voted early and often. A remedy for hoarseness was given away at the polling place, by a candidate who had several.
THE CENTENNIAL.—The city kept the hundredth year of General Washington's inauguration with three days of parades. A druggist on Broad street exhibited the President's false teeth, or a set of them.

THE OTHER HALF.—A police reporter has made a book of the tenements, with photographs taken by flash-light in the rooms at night. The ward has not read it; a druggist of Mulberry street has, and has taken his card out of one of the pictures.
BARNUM.—Mr. Barnum is dead at Bridgeport, the greatest showman of the age. The proprietors of remedies, who learned their trade from him, have put crape on their wagons.
THE ISLAND.—The new immigrant station on Ellis Island is open. Each arrival is examined by a physician; those found sickly are sent back, and the rest are sent to Mulberry street.
THE CHOLERA.—Ships from Hamburg are held at quarantine with cholera aboard. The druggists of the city report a run on every bottle with 'cholera' on the label, and some without.

THE COLUMBIAN PARADE.—The city kept the four hundredth year of Columbus with three days of parades, and the ward turned out under its flags. A druggist of Mulberry street sold a 'Discovery Tonic,' which he says is the first thing Columbus would have bought.
THE PANIC.—The banks are calling in their loans and the mills are shut. The ward has no money for medicine, and buys it anyway, on credit, from a man who has none either.
THE ELECTION.—The reform ticket has beaten the Hall, and the new Mayor promises to clean out the police. The druggists of the ward are waiting to see whether he means it.
THE POLICE BOARD.—Mr. Roosevelt walks the beats at night to catch his patrolmen asleep. He found two in a druggist's doorway, sleeping very soundly, and has asked what the druggist sells.

THE CAMPAIGN.—Mr. Bryan spoke for free silver at the Garden in the heat for two hours, and much of the crowd went home before he did. A proprietor of the ward has put out a Sixteen-to-One Tonic: sixteen parts water to one of the remedy.
THE TOMB.—General Grant's tomb is dedicated on Riverside Drive with a parade of many thousands. The proprietor of bitters who once offered to make up the fund sent a wreath, with his card.
THE FIRE AT ELLIS ISLAND.—The immigrant station has burned to the ground in the night, and the old records with it. Nobody was hurt; the steerage is to land at the Barge Office again.

THE ELECTION.—The Hall has carried the first election of the Greater City, and the ward kept it with bonfires. The druggists sold the remedy for the morning after at the old Manhattan price, the greater city not yet having reached it.
THE GREATER CITY.—Brooklyn, Queens and Staten Island are joined to New York at midnight. The druggists of Brooklyn are now in the same city as their creditors.
THE WAR.—The Maine is sunk in Havana harbor, and the papers are for war. Recruits in the Sixth Ward are offered a tonic 'for the climate of Cuba' at a soldier's discount.
SANTIAGO.—The Spanish fleet is destroyed off Santiago, and the city has surrendered. The druggists of the ward put out flags and a tonic 'for the heroes,' at a hero's price.

MONTAUK.—The soldiers come home from Cuba to the camp at Montauk with the fever, and their families go down to look for them. A proprietor has sent a carload of his tonic; the surgeons have sent it back.
THE DEWEY PARADE.—Admiral Dewey came up the Bay and down Fifth avenue, under an arch of plaster at Madison square. A proprietor of the ward has named a tonic for the Admiral, who has not been asked.

THE AUTOMOBILE SHOW.—Horseless carriages by the hundred, steam, electric and gasoline, are on show at the Garden. The cab horses on the rank outside are said to be taking it hard, and a druggist has advertised a remedy for them.

THE PRESIDENT.—President McKinley is dead at Buffalo of the assassin's bullet, and Mr. Roosevelt is President. A druggist of the Bowery who had advertised a 'Pan-American Tonic' has taken the card out of his window.
THE ELECTION.—The Fusion ticket has beaten the Hall, and Mr. Low is to be Mayor. A tonic called the Reform has been put up in the ward, and is said to be weaker than the old one.
THE ELECTION.—The Hall is back, and Mr. McClellan is Mayor. The druggists of the ward have taken the Reform tonic off the shelf, where it had not been disturbed.

THE SLOCUM.—The excursion steamer General Slocum burned in the East River with the Sunday school of a German church aboard, and more than a thousand are dead, most of them women and children. The life preservers were rotten, and some, it is said, had iron in them to make up the weight. The ward knows something of what is sold under a label, and is in mourning with Little Germany.

THE SUBWAY.—The underground railway is open from City Hall to Harlem in fifteen minutes. A tonic for the nerves of passengers is sold at every station but the first, whose passengers have not yet been down.
THE MAGAZINES.—Collier's prints 'The Great American Fraud,' naming the remedies and what is in them. The druggists of the ward report the article is very popular, and so, still, are the remedies.

THE CHAMPIONSHIP.—The Giants have beaten the Athletics of Philadelphia for the championship of the world, Mathewson pitching three games and giving up no run in any of them. A proprietor of the ward has named a liniment for his arm, without asking.

THE ELECTION.—Mr. Hearst ran for Mayor against the Hall and very nearly beat it, and the count is disputed. A proprietor of a nerve tonic who advertised in both camps reports a good result either way.
THE PACKING HOUSES.—A novel of the Chicago stockyards has put the city off its sausage. The proprietors of remedies, whose own works have not yet been written up, are reading it with great attention.
SAN FRANCISCO.—The city is shaken down and burned. A proprietor of the ward has sent a case of his remedy to the relief committee, which has asked him to send money instead.

THE MUCK-RAKERS.—The President says the magazine writers who expose the trusts are like the man with the muck-rake, who could look no way but down. The proprietors of the ward agree, and wish the writers would look the other way altogether.
THE PURE FOOD LAW.—Congress has passed, and the President signed, a law that every bottle shall say upon its label what is in it, from the first of January. The trade has six months to find out.

verdictLead: The bottle found at the bedside bore the label of {label}. Whether its proprietor spoke for his preparations or kept away, it did not detain the jury long. Physicians observe that the remedy is purely vegetable, and that so is hemlock.

verdictLead.text: A chemist from the College of Pharmacy gave evidence that the bottle of {label} contained, besides syrup and spirit, enough of a certain drug to quiet a dray-horse. The proprietor's advertisements describe it as gentle.

verdictLead: The jury retired for twenty minutes and returned with the label of {label} written into its verdict. The foreman remarked that he had a bottle of it at home, and would be pouring it away.
The bottle of {label} was passed along the jury, and each man smelled it. The foreman said afterward that the smell was evidence enough, and the chemist's report only confirmed it.

investmentNotices.branch_shop.bought: IN THE TRADE.—The proprietor of {product} has taken a corner shop in the Ninth Ward, fitted with counter and gas, and put a clerk in it. The Ninth Ward is said to be delighted, and has not yet been asked.
almanac.bought: IN THE TRADE.—Ten thousand copies of the proprietor's almanac are going about the city, with the moon's phases, a recipe for pickles and every claim on his label. The pickles are said to be reliable.
IN THE TRADE.—The proprietor's almanac for the year is out, with the tides, the eclipses, a page of jokes and the claims of {product}, of which the jokes are said to be the most believed.
IN THE TRADE.—A new almanac of {product} is to be had free at the shop and by post, with a calendar, a dream book and forty testimonials. The dream book is said to be the most accurate part.

almanac.bought.text: IN THE TRADE.—The almanac of {product} is printed again, ten thousand strong, with the Saints' days, the phases of the moon and the remedy for each. The printer of Ann street says it is his best seller after the Bible.

IN THE TRADE.—The proprietor of {product} has his almanac out again for the new year, with fresh testimonials, fresh jokes and the same claims, which the printer set from last year's type to save the trouble.

investmentNotices.wholesale_contract.bought: IN THE TRADE.—Messrs. Kittredge & Vail of Newark will take the goods of {product} by the dozen, for druggists in Paterson, Newark and Elizabeth. New Jersey is to be cured wholesale.
investmentNotices.laboratory.bought: IN THE TRADE.—A back room on Mulberry street has been fitted with retorts, and a German chemist installed who asks no questions. The neighbors have begun to ask some.
almanac.lapsed: IN THE TRADE.—The proprietor's almanac for the year is out of date, and is now chiefly used for lighting fires. It may be had again on application.
IN THE TRADE.—The year's almanac of {product} has run its course, and its predictions with it. The kitchens of the ward are said to be using it for curl-papers.
IN THE TRADE.—The almanac of {product} has had its year, and the last copies hang on nails in the privies of the ward, where they are read more closely than anywhere else.
investmentNotices.branch_shop.lost: IN THE TRADE.—The branch in the Ninth Ward has put up its shutters. The clerk is said to have taken the till, and the ward to have taken the clerk's side.
investmentNotices.wholesale_contract.lost: IN THE TRADE.—Messrs. Kittredge & Vail of Newark have cancelled their order for {product}, having read the papers. New Jersey will have to find its own remedies.
laboratory.mishap: FIRE.—A blaze in a back room on Mulberry street brought out Engine No. 9 on {weekday}. A quantity of ether was found to be the cause, and a German chemist the excuse. The proprietor's loss is put at twenty-five dollars, and the talk at a good deal more.

FIRE.—The laboratory behind the shop on Mulberry street took fire on {weekday} when a retort cracked over the gas. The chemist put it out with a wet sack; the loss is put at twenty-five dollars and the chemist's eyebrows.

FIRE.—Smoke was seen from the back of the shop on Mulberry street on {weekday}, and the engines came. The proprietor says it was an experiment; the neighbors that it was a fire; the loss, of twenty-five dollars, says the neighbors were right.

FIRE.—An explosion in the laboratory behind the shop on Mulberry street broke two windows on {weekday} and frightened a horse. The chemist is unhurt and says he has learned something; the loss is twenty-five dollars.

items.text: NEW YEAR'S.—Gentlemen made their calls on New Year's Day, two hundred houses apiece by some reports, and the druggists opened early the next morning for the headaches.

NEW YEAR'S.—The ladies of the avenue received from noon until ten, with eggnog in the parlor and the callers' cards on the hall table. A druggist of Fourteenth street did a large business on the second in a powder for the morning after, and a larger one on the third in a powder for the morning after that.
NEW YEAR'S.—The custom of the New Year's call is said to be dying out among the better sort, who leave cards instead. The ward keeps it up, and the druggists keep up with the ward.

items: NEW YEAR'S.—The bells of Trinity rang the old year out at midnight, and the horns of the Bowery rang it out again at one. Several of the ward have taken the pledge for the new year, and a proprietor of bitters reports that they have taken his bitters with it, as not being drink.

THE NEW YEAR.—The proprietors of the city have their almanacs out for the year, with the eclipses, the tides and a cure for each of the twelve months. The almanacs agree that the year will be an unhealthy one, which is what an almanac is for.

items.text: NEW YEAR'S EVE.—A crowd of several thousand stood in Broadway to hear the chimes of Trinity, and a smaller one stood at the druggist's on the corner next morning to hear the price of a headache powder.

THE NEW YEAR.—The Greater City saw the year in with horns from the Battery to the Bronx. The Health Department's last return for the old year shows the death rate lower and the druggists' books show their trade higher, and each takes the credit.

items: RESOLUTIONS.—The Temperance Society reports eleven hundred pledges signed in the ward on New Year's Day. A proprietor of bitters, asked for his view, said he welcomed every one of them, his bitters being a medicine.

items.text: THE NEW YEAR.—The saloons were open late and the churches early, and between them a druggist of Grand street sold a nerve tonic to both congregations. He says it is the only thing in the ward that unites them.

THE NEW YEAR.—The year was seen in at Times square by a crowd of many thousands, with horns, rattles and fireworks from the tower of the Times building. The druggists of Broadway opened early for headaches, as their fathers did after the New Year's calls.

NEW YEAR'S.—The Mayor received at the City Hall and shook hands with every caller until four, and the Aldermen with every caller who could be useful. A proprietor of the ward who called with a case of his tonic was received, and the tonic was not.

tails: The druggists opened early on the second, for the headaches.
The pledges taken at midnight were mostly broken by noon, and the rest by supper.
A proprietor of the ward has dated his testimonials for the new year, the old ones having been used.
The almanacs of the patent medicines were on every doorstep by morning, each promising the healthiest year yet to those who buy the bottle.
The Mayor is said to have been offered a remedy for the hand, and to have shaken that too.
The churches were full in the morning and the druggists' in the afternoon.
The Temperance Society took a hundred pledges, and a proprietor of bitters says he will honor every one.
A druggist of Grand street put up his prices for the new year, as he does every year, and says it is the only resolution he has ever kept.

items: ST. PATRICK'S DAY.—The parade went up Fifth avenue in the rain, as usual, and so did the spectators. The druggists of the Sixth Ward report a heavy trade on the eighteenth, in the usual remedy for the usual complaint.

ST. PATRICK'S DAY.—The societies marched to the Cathedral with green sashes and banners, and the Mayor reviewed them from the City Hall. A proprietor of the ward sold a bitters colored green for the day, and the color is said to have been the only thing in it that was not water.

items.text: ST. PATRICK'S DAY.—The parade passed the stand at the City Hall, where the Mayor and the Aldermen stood with their hats off for an hour and caught the usual colds. A druggist of Chambers street sent them a remedy, with his compliments and a bill.

items: THE SEVENTEENTH.—The shamrocks came over in a crate on the Umbria and were sold on Broadway at a cent the sprig. A druggist of Mott street sells a remedy for the morning of the eighteenth, which he says came over in the same crate.

items.text: ST. PATRICK'S DAY.—Forty thousand marched, the largest parade the Greater City has seen, and Brooklyn had one of its own besides. The druggists of both boroughs report the eighteenth the best day of the month, as usual.

items: ST. PATRICK'S DAY.—A proprietor of the Bowery has put out a 'Shamrock Tonic' for the day, and was asked by a policeman of the parade what was Irish in it. He said the label. The policeman said he had thought as much.

ST. PATRICK'S DAY.—The schools of the parish marched with the societies, and the band of the Catholic Protectory played. A druggist on the line of march stood in his door with a tray of remedies for sore feet, and sold them all to the band.

items.text: ST. PATRICK'S DAY.—Two of the Police Commissioners marched with the parade and two reviewed it, which the Board says is the only matter on which it has agreed this year.

ST. PATRICK'S DAY.—The Hall marched in silk hats behind its own band, and its district leaders were cheered on every corner where they had bought the beer. A proprietor of the ward who had not bought any was not cheered, and has asked the Hall what it costs.

The marchers' feet were seen to afterward by a druggist on the line of march, who had laid in a liniment for the purpose.

The bands played until dark, and a lozenge for the cornets was sold at the Cathedral door.

items.text: DECORATION DAY.—The veterans marched up Fifth avenue on Decoration Day, fewer than last year. A druggist on Broadway displayed in his window a liniment 'as used in the late War,' and a bottle of it, he says, that was.

DECORATION DAY.—The Grand Army posts marched to the cemeteries with flowers, and the soldiers' graves were dressed from Cypress Hills to Trinity churchyard. A proprietor of the ward, who was a sutler in the War, marched with them, and sells a tonic on the strength of it.

DECORATION DAY.—The posts of the Grand Army turned out with the drums, and the boys of the ward followed them to the ferry. The veterans' pensions are paid by the quarter, and the proprietors of the ward know the quarters better than the veterans do.

DECORATION DAY.—The parade was the shortest yet, the veterans being older and the day hotter. Two of them fell out at Madison square and were given water by the police and a tonic by a druggist, who sent the bill to the Post.

DECORATION DAY.—The veterans of the late War marched with the volunteers of the war with Spain behind them, and the boys of the ward could not tell which to cheer. A proprietor who sold a tonic to both armies has the testimonials of each in his window.

DECORATION DAY.—The wheelmen went out of the city by the thousand on the holiday and came back by the thousand in the evening, sunburnt and sore. The druggists of the Boulevard sold more liniment on the thirtieth than on any day of the year.
DECORATION DAY.—The flags were at half-mast until noon, as the custom is, and at the top afterward. The druggists of the ward kept their prices at the top all day.

DECORATION DAY.—The veterans march to-day, and the streets on the line of the parade are hung with flags. A druggist of Broadway has draped his window in black and filled it with liniment, and expects a good afternoon.
DECORATION DAY.—The Grand Army marches to-day, and the cemeteries will be full of flowers by evening. A proprietor of the ward who has sent a wreath to each post has had his card tied to it.

A proprietor of the Bowery sent each post a case of his tonic, and each post sent it on to the Soldiers' Home, which sent it back.
The pension agents walked with the crowd, and a proprietor of the ward who sells to pensioners walked beside them.
Several of the veterans fell out from the heat and were revived by a druggist on the line, who has asked the Post for a testimonial.
The fife and drum corps played the old tunes, and a lozenge for the fifes was sold at the corner.

items: THE FOURTH.—The ward celebrated with firecrackers from dawn. Three fingers were lost in Hester street; the druggists sold arnica by the pint, and a proprietor of a burn salve calls it the best Fourth he has had.

THE FOURTH.—The cannon crackers began at midnight and the ambulances at six. The hospitals dressed the usual burns and the usual hands; the druggists of the ward sold a salve for burns by the jar, and charged by the burn.

items.text: THE FOURTH.—The Tammany Society kept the day at the Wigwam with the reading of the Declaration and a long speech, and the braves went home in carriages. A druggist of Fourteenth street had a remedy ready at the door, and the Society has ordered a case for next year.

items: THE FOURTH.—The flags were out on every fire-escape in the ward, and a boy of Elizabeth street lit a pack of crackers in his father's coat. The father is doing well and the coat is not, and a druggist has sold the family a salve and a lecture.

items.text: THE FOURTH.—The physicians blame the toy pistol again for the lockjaw that follows the Fourth, and ask the shops not to sell it. The shops ask how they are to live, and the druggists have laid in a remedy for the lockjaw that is as good as the pistol is safe.

items: THE FOURTH.—The excursion boats were full to the rail and the beer gardens to the fence. Coney Island had its fireworks at nine and its sunburns all day, and the druggists of Surf avenue sold a remedy for each.

items.text: THE FOURTH.—The Fourth came on the heels of the news from Santiago, and the ward fired off everything it had, twice. A proprietor of the Bowery sold a 'Victory Tonic' from a cart hung with bunting, and was arrested for the bunting, which was the Navy Yard's.
THE FOURTH.—The papers report fewer deaths from the toy pistol this year than last, and credit their own campaign. The proprietors of lockjaw cures credit nothing, and report a dull Fourth.

items: THE FOURTH.—The Declaration was read from the City Hall steps to a crowd that could not hear it for the crackers. A druggist on Park row says he could hear his own till over both.

THE FOURTH.—The engines answered more alarms on the Fourth than in the week before it, chiefly for rockets on the roofs. A roof in Cherry street took fire from a pin-wheel, and a druggist across the way sold the tenants a remedy for the smoke before the engines came.

The toy pistol is blamed again by the physicians, and defended again by the shops that sell it.
The Declaration was read at the City Hall, and the crackers were heard better.
A proprietor of the ward fired a salute of twenty-one bottles from his doorstep, corks only, and had the corks printed with his name.
Several of the injured were dressed at the druggists' for want of an ambulance, and paid for it.

items.text: LABOR DAY.—The first Monday of September is a holiday by law this year, and the trades marched up Fifth avenue under their banners, the cigarmakers, the bricklayers, the typesetters and the rest. A druggist on the line of march, who employs two boys at a dollar a week, put out a flag.

LABOR DAY.—The unions marched in the morning and picnicked in the afternoon at Jones's Wood, where the speeches were long and the beer longer. A proprietor of the ward sold a tonic 'for the working man,' at a price the working man could not reach without a strike.

items: LABOR DAY.—The parade was smaller this year, the unions being on strike against one another. A proprietor of a nerve tonic says he sold to both sides, and is neutral.

items.text: LABOR DAY.—The holiday is a national one now, by act of Congress, and the President has said a word about it. The proprietors of the ward, who work everybody but themselves seven days a week, kept the shops open.

LABOR DAY.—The garment workers of the East Side marched with banners in Yiddish and English, and the sweaters watched from their windows. A druggist of Hester street sold a tonic for the overworked, and sold the most of it to the sweaters.

items: LABOR DAY.—The cloakmakers, the pants-makers and the pressers marched to Union square, and the speakers asked for the ten-hour day. A proprietor of the Bowery whose clerk works fourteen hours advertised a remedy for fatigue.
LABOR DAY.—The trades kept the holiday and the druggists did not. A proprietor of Grand street says the day of rest is the busiest of his year, the rest being taken mostly at his counter.

items.text: LABOR DAY.—Thirty thousand marched, the Mayor reviewed them, and the Hall's men marched beside them in silk hats. The druggists of the ward kept their boys at the counter, the holiday being, as one of them said, for those who work.

items.text: ELECTION DAY.—Mr. Hill is Governor by the returns on the bulletin boards of Park row, and the ward has carried its district for the Hall as usual. The saloons were shut by law until the polls closed; the druggists were not, and did the saloons' trade.

ELECTION DAY.—Mr. Hewitt is Mayor, Mr. George second and young Mr. Roosevelt third, and the Hall says the city has been saved. The workingmen say it has been counted. The druggists of the ward sold a remedy for disappointment to both sides, and kept one back for Mr. Roosevelt.

ELECTION DAY.—The new ballot law was tried for the first time, every man marking his ticket alone in a booth, and the captains of the ward were greatly put out. Mr. Grant is Mayor again. A druggist of Mott street, who used to carry the ward's tickets to the polls by the bundle, now sells it a remedy for the booth.

ELECTION DAY.—Mr. Flower is Governor, and the Hall has the state. A proprietor of the Bowery named his tonic for the new Governor before the polls closed, and would have named it for the other man had the returns gone the other way.

ELECTION DAY.—Mr. Cleveland is President again, and the bonfires burned on every corner of the ward until dawn. A druggist who had bet on Mr. Harrison paid his bet in bottles, which the winner says is the second time he has lost.

ELECTION DAY.—Mr. McKinley is President, and gold has beaten silver. The returns were thrown on a sheet on the Herald building, and the crowd in the square cheered both sides by turns. A proprietor who put out a Sixteen-to-One Tonic in the summer has marked it down to one-to-one.
ELECTION DAY.—Colonel Roosevelt, home from Cuba, is Governor by a narrow count. The Rough Riders' Tonic, which a proprietor of the Bowery put out in August, has been put up a nickel.

ELECTION DAY.—Mr. McKinley is President again, with Governor Roosevelt to be Vice-President, which the party's managers at Albany are said to be very glad of. The returns were signalled by searchlight from the tower of the Garden, and a druggist of the square sold a remedy for the eyes.

ELECTION DAY.—Governor Odell is returned by the up-State vote, and the city voted the other way, as usual. The druggists of the ward report the night's bonfires the largest in years, and the morning's headaches in proportion.

ELECTION DAY.—Mr. Roosevelt is President in his own right, and Judge Parker has gone back to the law. The crowd in Herald square cheered the returns until two, and a proprietor sold it a lozenge for the voice at a penny.

ELECTION DAY.—Mr. Hughes, who looked into the insurance companies, is Governor, and Mr. Hearst is not. The proprietors of remedies, who will have the new law looking into them from January, are said to have voted for whoever seemed least likely to look.

items: ELECTION DAY.—The ward voted early, and the Hall's men saw to it that it voted often. The saloons were shut by law until the polls closed, and the druggists, who are not, did the saloons' trade in the saloons' bottles.

ELECTION NIGHT.—The boys of the ward burned their bonfires on election night with every barrel, box and wagon not nailed down. A druggist of Mott street, whose shutters went on the fire, says he voted the other way.

ELECTION DAY.—The returns were thrown on a sheet in Printing House square by the stereopticon, and the crowd cheered every figure, not knowing whose it was. A proprietor of the ward threw his own advertisement on the sheet between the returns, and was cheered too.

ELECTION DAY.—The polls of the ward were kept in a barber's shop, a cigar store and a stable, and a druggist of Elizabeth street has applied to keep one next year, the stable having done so well by it.

items.text: THANKSGIVING.—The ragamuffins were out on Thanksgiving Day in their fathers' coats and false faces, begging pennies from door to door. A druggist of the Bowery gave each a lozenge, and has had his window broken.

THE NEWSBOYS.—The Newsboys' Lodging House gave its dinner on Thanksgiving Day to four hundred boys, who ate everything set before them and a good deal that was not. A proprietor of bitters sent a case, which the Superintendent sent back.

THANKSGIVING.—The Governor's proclamation was read from the pulpits, and turkey went up two cents the pound in Washington Market. A druggist of the ward sold a remedy for dyspepsia on the Friday, at a price the turkey had not reached.

THANKSGIVING.—The missions of the Bowery gave their dinners to some thousands, and the Five Points House of Industry to its children. A proprietor of bitters sent a case to each, with his card, and each sent back the bitters and kept the card for the fire.
THANKSGIVING.—The football game at the Polo Grounds drew its thousands in silk hats and chrysanthemums, and a remedy for the cold was sold at the gate to those who had brought their own.
THANKSGIVING.—The football game at Manhattan Field drew twenty thousand in silk hats and chrysanthemums, and a remedy for the cold was sold at the gate to those who had brought their own.

THANKSGIVING.—The Sixth Ward dined on what it could get, and the charities on what they could give. A proprietor of the ward who gives nothing advertised a tonic 'to give thanks with,' at fifty cents.

THANKSGIVING.—The Salvation Army gave its dinner in the Grand Central Palace to four thousand, with a band. A proprietor of the Bowery sent round a man with his bills, who was fed, and stayed for the hymns.

THANKSGIVING.—The ragamuffins made their rounds in false faces, and the druggists of the ward gave each a lozenge. The lozenges were in the gutter by Saturday, the ragamuffins having found that they tasted of the shop.

items.text: CHRISTMAS.—The stores on Grand street were lit till ten in the week before Christmas. A druggist advertised a tonic as the ideal present for a mother-in-law, and has declined to say why.

CHRISTMAS.—The Sisters of the Foundling Asylum gave the children a tree, and the Newsboys' Lodging House gave its boys a dinner. A proprietor of the ward sent a crate of soothing syrup to the Asylum, and the Sisters sent it to the Board of Health, with a note.

CHRISTMAS.—The stores of Sixth avenue were open until eleven in Christmas week, and the shop-girls stood until they dropped. A proprietor sold the floorwalkers a tonic for the girls, at a reduction for the dozen.

CHRISTMAS.—The poor of the ward had their dinners from the missions, the district leader and the Salvation Army, in that order of noise. A druggist of the street gave each child a peppermint, with his card.

CHRISTMAS.—Holly and greens from the Jersey woods were sold on Fourteenth street, and the patent medicines put out their Christmas almanacs. One of them offers its remedy as 'a gift that keeps on giving,' and does not say what.

CHRISTMAS.—The Salvation Army's lasses stood at the corners with their kettles, and a proprietor of the ward stood beside one with his remedies until the lass asked him to move along. He says he will take a corner of his own next year.
CHRISTMAS.—Santa Claus was seen on Grand street in a cotton beard, handing out the bills of a cough remedy. Several children who asked him for a doll were given a bill.

CHRISTMAS.—The department stores of Sixth avenue lit their windows with electric lamps, and the crowd stood ten deep to see a doll walk. A proprietor of Grand street has put a doll in his own window, taking a spoonful of his remedy every minute, and the crowd stands two deep.

CHRISTMAS.—The Christmas trade in remedies was the heaviest for years, a bottle being, as one proprietor advertised, 'the present that shows you care.' Several were returned on the twenty-sixth, unopened.
CHRISTMAS.—It is Christmas morning, and the ward's stockings hang on the fire-escapes. A druggist of Mott street is open, as he says, for those who find coal in theirs.
CHRISTMAS.—The churches are full this morning and the shops are shut, all but the druggists', which keep the holiday in their own way, at holiday prices.

tails: A druggist advertised a tonic as the ideal present for an uncle, and has declined to say which uncle.
A proprietor of the ward has his Christmas almanac out, with a recipe for plum pudding and a remedy for it.
The druggists alone kept open on the day, at holiday prices.
A proprietor of the Bowery sent a case of his remedy to every alderman, and has had eleven notes of thanks and one bottle back.
The Santa Claus on Grand street handed out the bills of a cough remedy with his candy, and the children are said to have kept the candy.
The Christmas trade in remedies was brisk, a bottle making, as one proprietor advertises, a present that can be given again.
